import os, shutil
import h5py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def subsample_dataset(src_dir, dst_dir, frac=0.6, seed=0, max_cells=2000, max_features=5000):
    """Copy a dataset to a new name, keeping a random slice of it.

    Cells: a random ``frac`` of each file's cells, capped at ``max_cells``.
    Files sharing a cell count get the SAME kept-cell index, so modality files
    and their label CSVs stay aligned - which is exactly the property your own
    export pipeline must preserve. Features: files with more than
    ``max_features`` rows (peak matrices) keep a random subset, so the copy
    stays small and fast to write. The output is the canonical layout:
    matrix/data as features x cells, plus matrix/features and matrix/barcodes.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    os.makedirs(dst_dir, exist_ok=True)
    counts, keep = {}, {}
    for fn in sorted(os.listdir(src_dir)):
        p = os.path.join(src_dir, fn)
        if fn.endswith(".h5"):
            with h5py.File(p) as f:
                if "matrix/data" in f:
                    counts[fn] = f["matrix/data"].shape[1]   # features x cells
        elif fn.endswith(".csv"):
            counts[fn] = len(pd.read_csv(p))
    for n in set(counts.values()):
        k = min(max(50, int(n * frac)), max_cells)
        keep[n] = np.sort(rng.choice(n, size=k, replace=False))
    for fn, n in counts.items():
        sp, dp = os.path.join(src_dir, fn), os.path.join(dst_dir, fn)
        idx = keep[n]
        if fn.endswith(".csv"):
            pd.read_csv(sp).iloc[idx].to_csv(dp, index=False)
        else:
            with h5py.File(sp) as f, h5py.File(dp, "w") as g:
                grp = g.create_group("matrix")
                n_feat = f["matrix/data"].shape[0]
                fidx = np.arange(n_feat) if n_feat <= max_features else np.sort(rng.choice(n_feat, size=max_features, replace=False))
                block = f["matrix/data"][fidx, :] if n_feat > max_features else f["matrix/data"][()]   # one fancy index per h5py read
                grp.create_dataset("data", data=np.asarray(block)[:, idx])
                if "matrix/features" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("features", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/features"])[fidx])
                if "matrix/barcodes" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("barcodes", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/barcodes"])[idx])
    return dst_dir

docs.title: Diagonal integration¶
docs.text:
Diagonal integration is the hard case: RNA and ATAC come from different cells, with no pairing and no shared cell ids, so a method must align two populations through a shared feature space (for RNA + ATAC, gene-activity scores, computed upstream of this package by e.g. Signac or ArchR). If your RNA and ATAC come from the SAME cells (10x multiome), that is vertical integration - use that tutorial instead.

Reference dataset: D28 (6,408 RNA + 4,606 ATAC cells). The stored results shipped with these notebooks were produced on it, so every table here reproduces.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text: pip install multibench-sc is the whole install: the 1.3 MB wheel ships the method registry, the stored result tables, the env lockfiles and the reference metadata. The package alone runs this section, section 3 (scan) and sections 4-5. Running methods (section 2, and run_all in section 3) additionally needs their environments - prebuilt linux-64 archives that need no conda binary - on a Linux host. The flag cell decides: with INSTALL_ENVS = False (the default) Run all is safe anywhere - nothing is downloaded, and a run cell on a host without the environments prints one line and stands in the benchmark host's own results; set it True on Colab or a Linux machine to download the environments in section 2 and run the methods for real. The install cell pins numpy / pandas to what the interpreter already has, so pip never upgrades a host's stack, and defines tick, the recorder behind the timing table at the end of the notebook.

docs.title: Environments - only if you will run methods in this session¶
docs.text: Linux; 2 envs, at least 1.6 GB to download (2 of 2 archives measured); multibench env plan --methods iNMF,online_iNMF,scJoint prints the per-env sizes. The cell below does nothing unless INSTALL_ENVS = True; then it prints the download the dry run measures and installs the prebuilt archives for the methods this tutorial runs (iNMF, online_iNMF, scJoint) under mtb.config.DEFAULT.envs_dir (~/.cache/multibench/envs on a host without conda - the archives carry their own interpreters, and run activates a prefix directly, so no conda binary is needed, on Colab included; with conda present the prefix goes to its envs dir and conda run is the fallback: MULTIBENCH_RUN_MODE in the API reference). env.install skips anything already present. Other tiers are one flag away on the command line: multibench env install --category diagonal --packed --run (9 envs, at least 21.6 GB to download (9 of 9 archives measured); multibench env plan --category diagonal prints the per-env sizes), or no flag for the whole benchmark (29 envs; multibench env plan totals them). The archives are linux-64: on macOS / Windows a real install refuses (force=True / --force overrides), which is why the cell checks the platform too. Without the environments, section 3's scan and sections 4-5 work as they are.

docs.title: One call¶
docs.text: One call is the whole pipeline: resolve each method's inputs, run it in its own environment, load the embeddings, score them with scIB metrics. Here online_iNMF, iNMF, scJoint. online_iNMF is among the fastest methods here - run_sec in the summary is the measured time on our host. The cell first asks scan whether any of these methods has its environment here; where none does (a laptop, Colab with the flag off) it prints one line and stands in the benchmark host's own run_all outputs for D28 - mtb.data.fetch_outputs downloads the tree run_all wrote there (summary, long table and one embedding per method) and mtb.load_batch(..., methods=) reloads it, so the statuses, run times and the evaluate cell below are real. Offline, or before those outputs are published, a second fallback stands in the same methods from the package's own sweep of D28 (load_results(source="rerun"), the package's re-execution of every wired method - the paper's own tables are source="published"); either way one printed line says which path was taken and every cell below still renders.

docs.title: 3. Your own data¶
docs.text: The same three calls - scan, run_all, plot - on a folder the package has never seen. A dataset is a folder of flat files named by category:

docs.title: 4. Reading stored results¶
docs.text: Section 2 ran three methods; the package ships the full sweep for D28 - every wired method at default settings, hours of compute - so the paper's figures reproduce from stored results in seconds. load_results reads them back as the tidy frame mtb.plot.bubble takes, and every row says in its source column which sweep it came from. The paper's table for D28 holds 14 methods against 12 in the package's sweep, so the default source="published" would show 14 - every call in this notebook names its source.

docs.title: What runs on a dataset, and why not¶
docs.text: scan inspects a folder and reports every runnable method - and for the rest, the exact reason (missing file, missing environment, wrong layout). Nothing executes. From the shell, multibench scan DATASET --category CATEGORY prints the compact table (method, modalities, runnable, files_ok, env_ok, runtime_tier, reason); --columns all or --format csv|tsv|json gives every column - including command, the exact shell line run() would execute for every variant whose inputs resolve (the line to paste into a scheduler job; multibench run-all ... --dry-run prints the same table). Below, the rows the data admits (files_ok), with the environment gate next to them: env_ok is what this machine has, env_reason the install line for what it lacks, and runnable (both gates) stays empty until the environments exist.

docs.title: What each method exposes for tuning¶
docs.text: method_info(m)["supports"] lists a method's variants with how many hyperparameters each exposes on its command line; mtb.params_for(m, CATEGORY, modalities) names them, params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets them in run_all (--param METHOD:KEY=VALUE on the command line; multibench params METHOD prints the same table for every variant). An empty tunable is honest: many upstream scripts hardcode their hyperparameters, and this package never edits upstream code.

docs.title: What the registry knows about a method, and how to cite it¶
docs.text: method_info carries the upstream reference, repository and version next to the run metadata - availability says whether a public install can run it ('public', or 'benchmark-host-only' for SPIRAL, the one method whose script is not published), needs_labels is the any-variant flag (supports[i] has it per variant), and verbose=True adds the long audit notes plus verification, the recorded end-to-end run(s) behind status='verified' ({dataset, category, status, wall_s, ARI, baseline, verdict, note}); mtb.cite emits the benchmark entry plus one per method you ran.

docs.title: The metrics¶
docs.text:
Two families, matching the paper's grouping. All are higher = better, on [0, 1] except ARI (slightly negative at chance level).

family metrics what they measure clustering / bio-conservation ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI does the embedding separate the annotated cell types? batch correction ASW_batch, GC, iLISI (+ opt-in kBET) are the batches mixed within each cell type?

Batch metrics appear only when the dataset has real batches - their absence on a single-batch dataset is correct, not missing data. kBET is computed only when named (mtb.evaluate(..., metrics=["ASW_batch", "GC", "iLISI", "kBET"])) because it is much slower than the rest.

docs.title: Coverage of the paper¶
docs.text: scan() answers "what runs on this dataset"; this answers how many of the methods the paper benchmarks for diagonal the package wires at all. For each one it does not, the registry's own record is printed - the categories it is wired for and the tasks (mtb.list_tasks() vocabulary) its variants are registered under; no variant for this category means the paper scored it here through a task the package does not run.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶
docs.text: symptom meaning fix files_ok False: input files not found a required file is absent the reason names the exact file and lists what IS in the folder env_ok False that method's conda env is not built the reason carries the one-method multibench env install ... command ... looks like cells x features matrix stored transposed re-export with mtb.io.to_canonical / export_dataset a method FAILs in seconds wrong input representation or layout read res.failures.iloc[0]["error"] - the full command line and stderr tail are there a method TIMEOUTs slow, not broken raise timeout=; runtime tiers in scan are measured, not guessed label_order_confidence low several label files fit the cell count check label_order_candidates in the record batch metrics scored against the wrong batches batch_source="file_of_origin" is the label-file rule res.rescore(batch=my_vector) re-scores the stored outputs without re-running

docs.title: Next steps¶
docs.text:
• the other three tutorials: vertical, mosaic, cross
  • the hosted interactive explorer: https://shiny.maths.usyd.edu.au/scMultiBench/ - the full benchmark's rankings, browsable without installing anything
  • mtb.recommend(CATEGORY, modalities=[...]) - stored-result ranking with coverage made explicit; methods wired for the category but absent from the chosen source appear with grand_score NaN rather than vanishing
  • mtb.sweep(...) - one method over a range of one hyperparameter

docs.title: Where the time went¶
docs.text: Seconds per stage, as tick recorded them (the install line is ~0 on a kernel that already had the package):

docs.title: Discover methods
docs.text:
scMultiBench's registry holds 40 methods across four integration categories - the 40 benchmark methods, several of them registered for more than one scenario. Before you run anything, the discovery API answers the only question that matters at the start of a project: given the data I have and the task I care about, which methods can I actually use?

This page is pure metadata lookup - no method environments, no GPUs, no data on disk. Everything here is a fast, in-process query against the registry and the benchmark catalog.

TL;DR

import multibench as mtb

mtb.list_tasks()                     # ['batch', 'classification', 'clustering', ...]
mtb.list_methods(category="vertical")        # every method in a category
mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal",        # filter by what your data has
                 modalities=["rna", "atac"],
                 needs_labels=False)
mtb.method_info("SCALEX")            # env, atac kind, label needs, availability, reference, variants
mtb.recommend("vertical", modalities=["rna", "adt"])   # ranked from stored results
mtb.inputs_for("D28", "diagonal", "SCALEX")  # resolve benchmark input paths: (dataset, category, method)
print(mtb.cite(["SCALEX"]))          # the benchmark + the method, one line each (fmt="bibtex" for .bib)

docs.title: The four integration categories
docs.text:
Every method declares one or more categories describing the experimental design it integrates. Pick the row that matches your data, then filter within it.

Category Design Typical modalities vertical Paired, the same cells measured in several modalities RNA+ADT, RNA+ATAC, RNA+ADT+ATAC diagonal Unpaired, separate cells per modality, bridged by shared features RNA batch + ATAC batch mosaic Overlapping modalities tied together by a bridge dataset mixed, partially paired cross Several fully matched datasets integrated together replicate cohorts (and spatial slices)

Category is the first filter

A method written for paired CITE-seq (vertical) cannot consume an unpaired RNA + ATAC design (diagonal). Always pass category= first, it is the single largest constraint on what is applicable.

docs.title: List what exists
docs.text:
mtb.list_tasks() returns the sorted set of tasks declared across the registry, and mtb.list_methods() returns method ids, optionally narrowed by category.

import multibench as mtb

mtb.list_tasks()
# ['batch', 'classification', 'clustering', 'dimension_reduction', 'imputation', 'registration']

mtb.list_methods()                       # all 40 registry methods
mtb.list_methods(category="vertical")    # only paired-design methods
mtb.find_methods("diagonal", task="clustering")   # by task: a find_methods filter (list_methods(task=) raises TypeError)

A method's categories are derived from its variants (method_info(m)["supports"]), never declared separately, so list_methods(category=c), find_methods(category=c) and env plan --category c always agree: 18 vertical, 14 diagonal, 6 mosaic and 12 cross methods.

docs.title: Filter by what your data has
docs.text:
mtb.list_methods filters on category only. When you want to filter by the task, or by the shape of your data - which modalities you measured, how your ATAC is encoded, whether you have cell-type labels to supervise with - use mtb.find_methods (every filter after category is keyword-only):

mtb.find_methods(category: str | None = None, *, task: str | None = None,
                 needs_labels: bool | None = None, atac: str | None = None,
                 modalities: list[str] | set[str] | None = None, runnable: bool | None = None,
                 tunable: bool | None = None, available: bool | None = None) -> list[str]

A worked example - I have an unpaired RNA batch and an ATAC batch, I have no cell-type annotation, and I want a method that consumes both modalities:

mtb.find_methods(
    category="diagonal",
    modalities=["rna", "atac"],
    needs_labels=False,
)
# ['SCALEX', 'Portal', 'uniPort', ...]

How the filters combine

find_methods returns the methods matching all supplied filters; passing None (the default) disables a filter. category, modalities, needs_labels and atac are judged per variant: a method matches when one of its variants satisfies all four together, not when different variants satisfy different ones. So scMoMaT is listed for find_methods("vertical", modalities=["rna", "adt"], needs_labels=False) - its vertical variant takes no labels, only its mosaic one does - and Multigrate is not listed for find_methods("vertical", modalities=["rna", "atac"]), because its only ATAC-consuming variant is mosaic. modalities is a subset test on the matching variant - the modality types it consumes must be a superset of what you ask for, so ["rna"] is broad and ["rna", "atac"] is stricter. Role tokens are reduced to their base type ("atac_gas" means "atac", "rna1" means "rna") and "protein" is accepted for "adt". Every token is validated: a typo in category, task, atac or a modality raises ValueError naming the valid vocabulary instead of silently matching nothing, and a bare string where a list is expected (modalities="rna") raises TypeError with the list form. Methods that consume a whole directory (the four spatial registration methods) cannot be judged by modalities=: they are kept under any such filter with a UserWarning naming them (task= "registration" selects them); scBridge's modalities are derived from the bare filenames it reads (rna, atac).

The atac filter is about encoding, not presence: methods that consume ATAC do so either as a gene-activity matrix (atac="gene_activity", alias "gas") or as raw peaks (atac="peak", alias "peaks"). It is the representation the upstream script expects, which is not always what its role name suggests (moETM, scMM and iPOLNG take a role called atac_gas but consume peaks). If your ATAC is already summarised to gene activities, filter for it so you do not pick a peak-only method.

mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", atac="gene_activity")
mtb.find_methods(category="vertical", tunable=True)     # methods whose command line exposes a hyperparameter

needs_labels is derived from the variants' roles - a variant "needs labels" when it takes a cell-type-label (cty) file as a required input. The filter is per variant; method_info(m)["needs_labels"] is the any-variant flag (scMoMaT is True because of its mosaic variant) and method_info(m)["supports"][i]["needs_labels"] the per-variant answer.

available=True keeps the methods a public install can run; available=False lists the one whose script is not published - SPIRAL (method_info(m)["availability"] == "benchmark-host-only"; scan reports it not runnable with the reason benchmark-host-only: script not published). GPSA runs through a package driver (method_info("GPSA")["driver"]) and is public, like PASTE and PASTE2; all three registration methods are public:

mtb.find_methods(task="registration", available=True)   # ['GPSA', 'PASTE', 'PASTE2']

docs.title: Inspect a single method
docs.text:
mtb.method_info returns a flat dict combining the registry spec with the method's provenance (upstream reference, repository, version, a one-line summary) and optional catalog metadata. It is the fastest way to understand a method before you commit to running it.

mtb.method_info("SCALEX")
# {'id': 'SCALEX', 'language': 'python', 'categories': ['diagonal'],
#  'tasks': ['clustering', 'batch'], 'env': 'scmb_torch', 'atac': 'gene_activity',
#  'needs_labels': False, 'status': 'verified', 'availability': 'public', 'setup_hint': '',
#  'variants': ['tools_scripts/SCALEX/main_SCALEX.py'], 'driver': None,
#  'repo_url': 'https://github.com/jsxlei/SCALEX', 'version': '1.0.2',
#  'reference': {'doi': '10.1038/s41467-022-33758-z', 'title': 'Online single-cell data integration ...',
#                'authors': 'Xiong L, ...', 'journal': 'Nature Communications', 'year': 2022},
#  'notes': 'Online integration of heterogeneous single-cell datasets ... no labels needed.',
#  'supports': [{'category': 'diagonal', 'modalities': ['rna', 'atac_gas'],
#                'output_kind': 'embedding', 'n_tunable': 0, 'needs_labels': False}],
#  'params': {...}, 'fixed_in_script': {...}, 'upstream_knobs': {...}, 'upstream_url': '...'}
Field Meaning id canonical registry token (the name you pass to run) language python or r, determines the conda env conventions categories / tasks integration categories the method supports / tasks its output is scored on env conda env name; run orchestrates via conda run -n <env> atac "gene_activity", "peak", or None if it consumes no ATAC needs_labels derived, any-variant: does some variant take a label file as a required input? (supports[i]["needs_labels"] per variant) status verified = the command template was cross-checked against the upstream entrypoint and the method was executed end to end on a reference dataset (declared = wired, not run) availability public - every entrypoint is in the public scMultiBench repository, or a package driver (GPSA); benchmark-host-only - the entrypoint is an absolute path on the benchmark host, not published (SPIRAL; scan reports it not runnable) variants / supports the per-design entrypoints, and per variant: category, modalities, output kind, n_tunable, needs_labels reference, repo_url, version, notes upstream provenance (verbose=True adds notes_long, the upstream-knob audit prose, and verification) verification (verbose=True) the evidence behind status="verified": one {dataset, category, status, wall_s, ARI, baseline, verdict, note} per recorded run, from the shipped multibench/files/final_verification.tsv (status there is the run outcome - CHAIN_OK, CHAIN_OK_GRAPH_METHOD, RUN_OK_NO_EMBEDDING; verdict is DRIFT when a re-run left the ARI tolerance) params per variant: defaults, tunable, effective (what the wrapper emits)

The catalog columns of the published tables (deep_learning, output, ...) are one row per method in mtb.catalog.methods() (see below).

method_info(m)["runtime"] is what the method has been observed to cost ({"tier", "worst_sec", "observed": [{dataset, cells, sec, source}, ...]}) - the measurements behind scan()'s runtime_tier column:

mtb.method_info("SCALEX")["runtime"]
# {'observed': [{'cells': 11014, 'dataset': 'D28', 'sec': 2233, 'source': 'manual'}], 'tier': 'slow', 'worst_sec': 2233}

Each observation says where it came from (source: manual, summary_csv = the shipped re-run sweeps, verification = the shipped verification table); the table keeps the longest recorded time per (method, dataset), and cells is null where no run recorded the count. An unknown method id raises KeyError with a did-you-mean hint in every one of these functions; mtb.cite("SCALEX", "GLUE") takes ids one per argument (or one list), like the CLI, and prints one line per entry (fmt="bibtex" for .bib entries). For a benchmark dataset, mtb.inputs_for(dataset, category, method) - the same (dataset, category, ...) order as scan and run_all; the 0.2 (dataset, method, category) order raises TypeError - returns absolute paths and, when a method has several variants for the category, picks the one whose files are in the folder (mtb.params_for(method, dataset=...) does the same for the hyperparameter table; when none or several fit, both raise mtb.AmbiguousVariantError, a ValueError).

docs.title: Rank from stored results
docs.text:
mtb.recommend turns the shipped metric tables into a ranking for a category, with coverage made explicit - a method scored on 1 of 22 datasets is not a winner:

mtb.recommend("vertical", modalities=["rna", "adt"])
#   method  grand_score  n_datasets  n_datasets_total  coverage  needs_labels  runtime_tier  worst_sec ...

needs_labels there follows the category's variants (scMoMaT is False in a vertical ranking), as does the L badge of the bubble plot.

source="rerun" ranks the package's own re-run sweeps instead of the paper's tables; long_df=pd.concat([published, mine]) places your own method in the same ranking; metrics="batch" ranks on the batch-correction metrics (None, the default, ranks on the clustering family; "all" or a list of codes on exactly those). Nothing is hidden: every method wired for the category (find_methods(category, modalities=..., runnable=True)) that has no rows in the chosen source is appended with grand_score NaN, n_datasets 0 and coverage 0.0 after the scored rows, and ONE UserWarning lists the datasets dropped for having fewer than min_methods methods, the partial coverage, and the unscored methods (try source="rerun" when that source has them). The choices the ranking was made under travel with the frame as df.attrs (metrics, family, source, not_scored, missing) - pandas keeps .attrs through .copy() and column selection but most concat / merge operations drop them, so the NaN rows themselves are the robust signal.

docs.title: The full benchmark catalog
docs.text:
mtb.catalog.* exposes the benchmark metadata as tidy DataFrames, useful when you want the whole picture rather than a single lookup.

from multibench import catalog

catalog.methods()    # one row per method: language, deep_learning, atac, output,
                     # needs_labels, categories, tasks (registry-derived), + canonical_id
catalog.datasets()   # one row per dataset: dataset, simulated, category, has_results, ...
catalog.metrics()    # the metric-details table

catalog.datasets() is the union of the paper's dataset table (63 real + 8 simulated, 71 ids) and every dataset id that has a stored result table - 80 rows today, the extra nine being ids that exist only as result tables (the D11s / D28s / D45s / D52s re-run subsamples, D24, SD7-SD10); category and has_results are filled from the shipped result tree at call time, and the simulated flag (set for ids beginning SD) separates the simulations:

ds = catalog.datasets()
ds[~ds["simulated"]]    # real datasets only

Two helpers normalise the catalog's free-text spellings to canonical tokens:

catalog.canonical_id("Seurat v5")     # 'Seurat_v5'
catalog.canonical_id("scipenn")       # 'sciPENN' - case-folded against the registry
catalog.canonical_metric("kbet")      # 'kBET'
catalog.known_metrics()               # the ten scIB codes + 'PCR'

An unknown name comes back unchanged; canonical_id(name, strict=True) raises KeyError with a did-you-mean hint instead (what load_results uses).

docs.title: Which method should I use?
docs.text:
A practical decision path tied to the four categories:

  1. Start from your design. Paired cells -> category="vertical"; unpaired modalities bridged by features -> "diagonal"; partially overlapping with a bridge -> "mosaic"; replicate matched datasets -> "cross".
  2. Filter by data shape. find_methods(category=..., modalities=[...], atac=..., needs_labels=...) - drop methods that need labels you do not have, or an ATAC encoding you cannot provide.
  3. Rank what is left. recommend(category, modalities=[...]) orders the candidates from stored results and shows the runtime tier next to the score.
  4. Check your folder. mtb.scan("MYDATA", category) reports, per method, whether the files are right (files_ok) and whether its environment is installed (env_ok) - then run_all.
candidates = mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", modalities=["rna", "atac"],
                              needs_labels=False)
mtb.recommend("diagonal", modalities=["rna", "atac"])[["method", "grand_score", "coverage", "runtime_tier"]]

Where to go next

  • Run a chosen method end-to-end: Run a method, or the category tutorials for run_all.
  • Score an output with scIB metrics: Evaluate a run.
  • Compare methods across datasets: Load & plot results.

Next: pick a method and run it end-to-end in Run a method.

docs.title: Multi-Task Omics — multibench end-to-end tutorial¶
docs.text:
This notebook walks the complete user story for the multibench wrapper around the scMultiBench integration methods:

inputs_for  →  params_for  →  run  →  evaluate  →  plot
 (data)        (tuning)      (method)  (metrics)   (figure)

Everything here is run-verified on one reference dataset, D11 (CITE-seq PBMC, 2,864 cells, RNA + ADT). All 14 methods that support the vertical [rna, adt] scenario were executed end-to-end on it.

Why D11? Integration methods are defined by the scenario they solve, so no single dataset can exercise all 40 methods. D11 is the largest set of methods (14) that share one dataset, and at 2,864 cells it is small enough that you can actually re-run this notebook.

docs.title: 0. Setup¶
docs.text: Run this notebook in the driver environment (scmbench_eval).

docs.title: Environments¶
docs.text:
Each method runs in its own conda environment (they need mutually incompatible framework versions). The package maps method → env for you, and ships lockfiles so a fresh machine can rebuild them.

multibench env doctor          # what is needed / missing
multibench env install --run   # build everything from lockfiles

docs.title: 1. Discovery — which methods fit my data?¶
docs.text: find_methods filters the registry; method_info describes one method.

docs.title: 2. Data — resolve the inputs¶
docs.text: inputs_for maps a dataset + method + scenario to the concrete files that method expects. check=True verifies they exist, so you fail fast instead of mid-run.

docs.title: 3. Parameters — what can I actually tune?¶
docs.text:
params_for reports two things:

  • defaults — parameters the wrapper passes on every run. Override them with run(..., params={...}).
  • tunable — parameters the upstream script accepts on its command line, with their upstream defaults.

An honest limitation. Only the parameters a method exposes on its CLI can be tuned, because this project never modifies the upstream method scripts. Of the 14 methods here, 5 expose hyperparameters; the other 9 hardcode them and report tunable: {}. That is a property of the methods, not a gap in the wrapper.

docs.title: 4. Run a method¶
docs.text:
run builds the command, executes it inside the method's own conda env, and loads the output back. Method scripts are never modified.

We pass params={"epochs": 5} to keep this demo quick — that is the tuning API from the previous section doing real work.

docs.title: ⚠️ Not every method returns an embedding¶
docs.text:
Check output.kind before you compute embedding-based metrics. Of these 14 methods, 12 return embedding and 2 return graph:

method kind what it writes Seurat_WNN graph a weighted nearest-neighbour graph — no embedding at all scMoMaT graph KNN indices/distances; a 2-D UMAP lives in extra_outputs

Running clustering metrics on a KNN index matrix silently produces garbage (ARI ≈ 0), so branch on kind rather than assuming.

docs.title: 5. Evaluate — scIB metrics¶
docs.text: evaluate derives an optimal-resolution Leiden clustering from the embedding and scores it against the true cell types (the standard scIB protocol). Pass the label vector in the embedding's cell order.

docs.title: 6. Plot¶
docs.text: to_long reshapes the scores for plotting; plot.bubble renders the comparison figure used throughout the benchmark.

docs.title: 7. Comparing all 14 methods¶
docs.text: Running every method takes hours (sciPENN 143 s → scMSI 2.3 h), so we load the verified results from the full sweep and plot them together.

docs.title: Reading the results¶
docs.text:
• Matilda (ARI 0.924) and totalVI (0.821) lead on this dataset.
  • scMSI (0.752) scores well but needs 2.3 h — it is CPU-only (its framework predates this GPU) and its self-expressive step is O(N²).
  • scMoMaT (0.447) is scored through its 2-D UMAP, which costs resolution — a consequence of it being a graph method, not a defect.
  • Seurat_WNN is absent from the plot on purpose: it emits only a graph, so embedding-based clustering metrics do not apply to it.

Scores are dataset-specific — do not read this as a global ranking.

docs.title: 8. The other integration scenarios¶
docs.text:
Integration methods are defined by which scenario they solve, so no single dataset can exercise all of them. Each scenario gets its own reference dataset:

scenario what the data looks like reference methods run vertical one cell, several modalities measured together D11 (2,864) 14 / 14 diagonal RNA and ATAC from different cells D28 (11,014) 9 / 9 mosaic several batches, only some overlap in modality D45 (32,151) 4 / 4 cross several batches sharing a modality D52 (23,478) 8 / 8

The API call is identical in every case — only category and modalities change.

docs.title: ⚠️ Trap 1 — label ORDER, the most dangerous silent failure¶
docs.text:
evaluate needs the label vector in the embedding's cell order. When a method stacks several batches, that order is a property of the method, and matching by length cannot detect a wrong order — every permutation has the same length. You get a number, no error, and it is wrong.

StabMap on D52 is the cautionary example. It puts its reference batch first (reference="data3"), so the correct order is cty3 + cty1 + cty2:

label order ARI cty3+cty1+cty2 (correct) 0.688 cty3+cty2+cty1 0.110 cty1+cty2+cty3 (naive sort) 0.0006

A naive sort makes a perfectly good method look completely broken. The same trap applies to diagonal methods that stack RNA-then-ATAC.

Verifying the stacking order of every diagonal method on D28 makes the point — the wrong order collapses every method to ~0.000x, so the correct one is unambiguous:

method rna→atac atac→rna scJoint 0.618 0.001 SCALEX 0.574 0.000 uniPort 0.001 0.599 ← the only ATAC-first method Conos 0.000 0.001 ← genuinely ~0 in both (2-D layout)

uniPort alone stacks ATAC first; naive rna+atac labelling reports 0.0009 for it. Conos scoring ~0 under both orders is what tells you its low score is real (its output is a 2-D layout) rather than another alignment bug.

On D52 the same trap hit two methods, and a third acts as the control:

method best order ARI (best) ARI (naive sort) StabMap cty3+cty1+cty2 0.688 0.0006 Concerto cty3+cty1+cty2 0.674 0.0008 totalVI cty1+cty2+cty3 0.767 0.767 ← sorted really is correct here

totalVI matters: it shows the naive order is sometimes right, so the order genuinely has to be determined per method rather than assumed either way.

run_any.py now does this automatically — it enumerates every length-matching order (including all permutations), scores each, keeps the best, and records the full spread in label_order_candidates so the choice stays auditable.

docs.title: ⚠️ Trap 2 — the bubble chart is a ranking, not absolute values¶
docs.text:
plot.bubble encodes radius = rank and fill = value normalised within the plotted set. Both are relative to whatever you plotted, so the same method can look dominant in one figure and mediocre in another.

That is the right encoding for a benchmark of many methods, but it exaggerates small gaps: on D52, sciPENN (0.6947), UINMF (0.6905) and StabMap (0.6880) are separated by 0.007 ARI yet occupy visibly different bubbles. Always read the summary table beside the figure.

docs.title: Runtime is the real constraint¶
docs.text:
Some methods need hours even on small data — they predate this GPU and run on CPU, or scale poorly:

method dataset runtime sciPENN D11 (2,864) 143 s scJoint D28 (11,014) 209 s sciCAN D28 (11,014) 4.4 h scMSI D11 (2,864) 2.3 h MultiVI D45 (32,151) 3.3 h

A sweep "timeout" is therefore not a failure — budget hours for the CPU-bound methods before concluding anything is broken.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
Step API pick a method find_methods, method_info resolve data inputs_for, labels_for inspect tuning params_for run run(..., params={...}) metrics evaluate, to_long figure plot.bubble environments mtb.env.*, multibench env doctor/install

Two things to remember

  1. Check output.kind before computing embedding metrics — 2 of these 14 methods return graphs.
  2. params_for tells you what is genuinely tunable; a method reporting tunable: {} hardcodes its hyperparameters upstream.

docs.title: Evaluate a run
docs.text:
You have a run output - a joint embedding - and a set of cell-type labels. Now you want a number. mtb.evaluate takes that output and returns the scIB metrics that the scMultiBench paper reports, in a metric.csv-shaped frame you can read, save, or feed straight into a bubble plot.

TL;DR

import multibench as mtb

metrics = mtb.evaluate(
    result.output,                        # embedding: ndarray / DataFrame / AnnData / .h5 / .npy / .csv
    labels=mtb.labels_for("D11")["cty"],  # one label per cell, in the embedding's row order
    metrics="clustering",                 # ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI (the default None: every applicable metric)
    # clustering= is optional - omitted, scIB's optimal-resolution Leiden
    # clustering is derived from the embedding
)
print(metrics)                            # index = metric, column "Value"

docs.title: What evaluate does
docs.text:
mtb.evaluate(output, labels=None, *, category=None, batch=None, metrics=None,
             clustering=None, obsm="X_emb", label_order=None, verbose=True) -> pd.DataFrame

output and labels are the two positional parameters; everything else is keyword-only.

Cost. ARI, NMI and iF1 need scIB's optimal-resolution Leiden sweep (ten resolutions on a kNN graph of the embedding): tens of seconds for a few thousand cells, minutes for ~10^4. evaluate announces the sweep with one stderr line when it starts on more than 2,000 cells (verbose=True, the default; False never prints); clustering= (your own assignment) or a metrics=[...] list naming only metrics that do not need it (ASW, iASW, cLISI, the batch family) skips it entirely.

Under the hood it assembles a small AnnData carrying your embedding in obsm["X_emb"], with celltype, cluster, and batch as observation columns, builds a neighbour graph on the embedding, and runs the scIB metric functions over it. The result is a DataFrame indexed by metric name with a single "Value" column, the same shape as the metric.csv files the benchmark ships. The index uses the canonical metric spelling load_results uses (ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI, ASW_batch, GC, iLISI, kBET), so a to_long frame concatenates with a stored table without duplicate metric columns - and it is never empty: a request that would select no metric raises instead of returning nothing.

metrics= is the one selection knob - the same vocabulary load_results and recommend take:

metrics= Metrics computed None (default) every applicable metric: the clustering family, plus the batch family when a batch vector exists (batch=, or labels as a list of two or more files) "clustering" ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI "batch" ASW_batch, GC (graph connectivity), iLISI - needs a batch vector "all" both families - needs a batch vector ["ARI", "ASW_batch", ...] exactly these codes (alias tolerant); kBET is computed only this way

category (vertical, diagonal, mosaic, cross) is optional: it is validated when given (a typo raises ValueError listing the four), but the metrics do not depend on it. metrics= selects a metric family, not a mtb.list_tasks() token: metrics="dimension_reduction" raises ValueError saying so (that task shares the clustering family).

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
evaluate is honest about what each metric group needs, and raises early if something is missing.

Clustering metricsBatch metrics

labels is required; clustering is optional - clustering quality is measured by comparing predicted clusters against the ground-truth cell types, and the clusters are derived for you when you do not pass any.

metrics = mtb.evaluate(
    result.output,
    labels="data/D11/cty.csv",   # single-column CSV, one header line, one label per cell
    metrics="clustering",
    # clustering="cluster.h5"    # optional: a precomputed clustering (h5 dataset
                                 # /obs/cluster_leiden, or any label-like input)
                                 # skips the internal Leiden sweep
)

Batch correction is scored against a batch vector, so metrics="batch" (and "all") additionally require batch - unless labels is a list (or an ordered dict) of two or more files, in which case each cell's file of origin (1, 2, ...) is the batch, the rule run_all applies (see below). The default metrics=None adds the batch family exactly when such a vector exists.

metrics = mtb.evaluate(
    result.output,
    labels=mtb.labels_for("D52"),     # {cty1, cty2, cty3} in the benchmark's cell-stacking order
    metrics="all",                    # (or leave metrics=None: three files -> both families)
    # batch=my_batch_vector           # overrides the file-of-origin rule
)

mtb.labels_for(ds) returns the files in the order the methods stack the cells (cty; cty1, cty2, ... numerically; rna_cty before atac_cty; labels_for(ds, category, method) follows that variant's own modality order), so the dict plugs in directly. A dict you built in any other order raises; pass label_order=["cty1", "cty2", "cty3"] - the keys in the method's stacking order, numbered files ascending and rna before atac, NOT alphabetical - or a list of paths in that order. Passing batch= with metrics="clustering" computes no batch metric and says so with a UserWarning; metrics="all" or "batch" without any batch vector raises ValueError (batch labels required for metrics='all' ...).

Every input can be a path or an in-memory object:

  • output - a numpy.ndarray (cells x dims; a dims x cells array whose other axis matches the label count is transposed for you, with a warning), a pandas.DataFrame, an AnnData (.obsm[obsm], default "X_emb"), a scipy sparse matrix, or a path: .h5 (dataset data, the benchmark's embedding.h5), .h5ad, .npy, .csv / .tsv. A path that does not exist raises FileNotFoundError naming the path and the current working directory; an .h5 without a data dataset raises ValueError listing the keys it found (and says so when the file looks like a canonical input matrix - matrix/data - rather than an embedding).
  • labels / batch / clustering - a CSV path (header row; column x, the only column, or the last of two behind a barcode index - for a file with several columns pass the column itself, pd.read_csv(p)["col"]), a list of CSV paths concatenated in that order, a dict as returned by mtb.labels_for (one entry, or several in the stacking order labels_for returns - otherwise label_order=), a 1-D array / Series / Categorical / list, a single-column DataFrame, or - when output is an AnnData (or a .h5ad path, read as one) - the name of an obs column, for clustering too. Values are compared as strings, so integer codes and names score identically.

Row order: positional, or aligned by cell id

Arrays, lists and files are matched positionally to the rows of output. A Series / DataFrame with a non-default index is aligned by cell id when output carries ids - an AnnData (obs_names) or a DataFrame with a non-default index: rows are reindexed to the output's order, and a missing or extra id raises ValueError naming the first offenders. Against a bare array there is nothing to align with, so the Series is matched positionally and a UserWarning says so - pass labels.to_numpy() to silence it, or an AnnData / DataFrame with ids to align. A Series with the default RangeIndex is positional and silent.

Missing labels raises

evaluate without labels raises ValueError (every family scores against the cell types); metrics="batch" / "all" without batch (and without a multi-file labels list) raises ValueError too, and a length mismatch says exactly what it saw (input length mismatch: emb has 2863 cells, celltype has 2864). These are programmer errors, not missing optional metrics - see graceful degradation below for the latter.

docs.title: Restricting what is computed
docs.text:
A metrics=[...] list names the metrics you want (a list, not a bare code - metrics="ARI" raises ValueError pointing at metrics=["ARI"]; an unknown code raises ValueError listing the vocabulary, mtb.plot.CLUSTERING_METRICS + mtb.plot.BATCH_METRICS; an empty list raises). Everything else is skipped, including the Leiden sweep when no requested metric needs it - ARI and NMI compare the derived clustering against the labels (pass clustering= to score your own and skip the sweep) and iF1 scores every resolution of it, so those three run the sweep; ASW, iASW and cLISI do not:

mtb.evaluate(result.output, labels=labels, metrics=["ASW"])            # no Leiden sweep, ~seconds
mtb.evaluate(result.output, labels=labels, clustering=my_clusters,
             metrics=["ARI", "NMI"])                                   # your clustering, no sweep
mtb.evaluate(result.output, labels=labels, batch=batch,
             metrics=["ARI", "ASW_batch", "GC"])                       # across both families

A listed batch metric (ASW_batch, GC, iLISI, kBET) needs batch= (or a multi-file labels): without one it raises ValueError: batch labels required for batch metric(s) ['GC']: pass batch=<vector> ... instead of returning an empty frame. kBET (shells out to R via rpy2; hours on large datasets) is never implicit - it is computed only when a list names it: metrics=["ASW_batch", "GC", "iLISI", "kBET"].

docs.title: Are my numbers comparable?
docs.text:
The metrics in the shipped tables and the metrics evaluate returns are computed the same way, so yes - provided you feed the same things:

  • labels - the dataset's cty CSV(s), one label per cell in the embedding's cell order. mtb.labels_for(ds) returns them ({"cty": ...} for single-label datasets, {"rna_cty", "atac_cty"} for diagonal, {"cty1", "cty2", ...} per batch) in the benchmark's cell-stacking order, so labels=mtb.labels_for(ds) is the whole recipe for a multi-file dataset; a dict in any other order needs label_order=.
  • clustering - omitted, scIB's optimal-resolution Leiden: ten resolutions from 0.2 to 2.0 on the embedding's neighbour graph, keeping the one with the highest NMI against the labels. Pass clustering= to score your own.
  • metrics - the scib.metrics functions; iASW / iF1 score every label (the isolated-label threshold is set to the batch count + 1, so no label is excluded).
  • cLISI / iLISI - need scib's compiled LISI helper (knn_graph.o). The shipped binary is Linux x86-64; when it cannot run (macOS, another architecture) evaluate rebuilds it in place once, with scib's own build line, if g++ / c++ / clang++ is on PATH, and only otherwise records NaN with a warning that carries the exact g++ command (see Installation).

docs.title: Batch vector on multi-batch layouts
docs.text:
run_all scores batch metrics against the label file each cell came from: cty1.csv -> 1, cty2.csv -> 2 (cross / mosaic), rna_cty.csv -> 1, atac_cty.csv -> 2 (diagonal) - the winning permutation is recorded in summary.label_order, and summary.batch_source says file_of_origin. Batches within one file (donors inside rna.h5, say) are therefore not represented. When your dataset has them, re-score with the vector it really has - nothing is re-run:

res = mtb.run_all("MYDATA", "cross", out_dir="out/", batch=my_batch_vector)   # at run time, or
res2 = res.rescore(batch=my_batch_vector)          # on the stored outputs; batch_source becomes 'user'
mtb.evaluate(Path(res.results[0]["out_dir"]) / "embedding.h5",               # one stored output
             labels=labels, batch=my_batch_vector, metrics="batch")

docs.title: Re-runs are stochastic
docs.text: Most methods are non-deterministic, so a re-run does not reproduce the stored decimals. The package ships every verification run (multibench/files/final_verification.tsv; read it per method with mtb.method_info(m, verbose=True)["verification"] - a list of {dataset, category, status, wall_s, ARI, baseline, verdict, note}, where baseline is the ARI recorded when the method was first verified and verdict is DRIFT when the re-run leaves the tolerance): on D11, 11 of 13 methods re-scored within ~0.02 ARI of their baseline, while VIMCCA moved 0.599 -> 0.695 and Concerto 0.408 -> 0.498. Compare ranks, not decimals, and prefer aggregate="summary" over several datasets when ordering methods.

docs.title: Graceful degradation
docs.text:
A few scIB metrics depend on external machinery that is not always present. Rather than failing the whole evaluation when one optional metric cannot run, evaluate computes each metric defensively: if it raises, the metric is recorded as NaN with a warning, and every other metric still returns.

Metric Needs If unavailable cLISI, iLISI scib's compiled LISI helper rebuilt in place when a C++ compiler is on PATH; else NaN + warning (with the rebuild command) kBET R via rpy2, and being named in metrics=[...] NaN + warning

So on a machine without the LISI binary and without a compiler, a single-batch call still gives you real ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, and iF1, only cLISI comes back NaN.

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
>>> metrics
       Value
ARI    0.812
NMI    0.847
ASW    0.591
iASW   0.604
iF1    0.733
cLISI    NaN     # LISI binary not runnable here and no compiler to rebuild it

It is a plain DataFrame, so you can save it as the benchmark's metric.csv directly:

metrics.to_csv("metric.csv")

docs.title: Closing the loop: tidy -> bubble plot
docs.text:
The wide "Value" frame is the right shape for one run. To compare across methods and datasets, and to draw the scIB-style bubble table from the paper, reshape it to the long frame that plot.bubble and load_results use, with mtb.to_long:

mtb.to_long(value_df, *, method, dataset=None, category=None,
            clustering="default", source="user") -> pd.DataFrame
# columns: metric, value, method, dataset, category, clustering, source

to_long emits the same seven columns load_results returns - source is "user" unless you say otherwise, so your rows stay distinguishable after a concat; method is required and keyword-only, and an omitted dataset / category is written as all / user rather than left blank - and maps each metric name to its canonical form (raising if two rows collapse onto the same name, so nothing is double-counted); evaluate already emits the canonical spelling, so the result lines up with mtb.load_results and can be concatenated with the stored tables without duplicate metric columns. A needs_labels column you add to the frame (mine["needs_labels"] = True) gives your (supervised) method the bubble table's L badge. It accepts evaluate's frame, a Series, or the CSV read back with a metric column; a frame that is already long, or one without a Value column, is rejected with a message naming the shape (and the df.T.set_axis(["Value"], axis=1) fix for a one-row frame).

import pandas as pd
import multibench as mtb

mine = mtb.to_long(metrics, method="SCALEX", dataset="D28", category="diagonal")
bench = mtb.load_results("diagonal", dataset="D28", source="rerun")   # the package's re-run sweep

fig = mtb.plot.bubble(
    pd.concat([bench, mine]),
    metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "GC"],   # this column order, left to right
    title="Diagonal integration, D28 + SCALEX",
    save="bubble.pdf",
)

plot.bubble returns a Matplotlib Figure (circle radius tracks rank, fill tracks value, one Overall bar per metric family). See the plotting tutorial for the full set of options, including published vs re-run tables.

The scIB metrics are the only metrics

metrics= selects among the ten scIB codes and their two families - registration metrics are not wired into evaluate (see Spatial registration), and any other token raises ValueError naming the vocabulary. The 0.2 task= / family= / only= spellings still work for one release with a DeprecationWarning; slow_metrics=, metric_set= and column= raise TypeError naming the replacement - see the API reference.

Next: turn these numbers into a figure in Load & plot results.

docs.title: Mosaic integration
docs.text:
In [1]: Copied! 
import importlib.metadata, importlib.util, sys, time
_t, TIMES = [time.time()], []                    # "where the time went": tick(label) records the seconds since the previous tick
def tick(label): TIMES.append((label, round(time.time() - _t[0], 1))); _t[0] = time.time()
if importlib.util.find_spec("multibench") is None:
    # pin numpy / pandas to what this interpreter already has, so pip never upgrades the host's stack (Colab pins pandas itself)
    pins = [f"{p}=={importlib.metadata.version(p)}" for p in ("numpy", "pandas") if importlib.util.find_spec(p)]
    !{sys.executable} -m pip -q install "multibench-sc>=0.3" {" ".join(pins)}   # registry, stored tables, env lockfiles and references ship in the wheel - no clone needed
    importlib.invalidate_caches()
    if importlib.util.find_spec("multibench") is None:        # PyPI behind the docs? take the same code straight from GitHub
        !{sys.executable} -m pip -q install "git+https://github.com/DSichang/scMultiBench.git" {" ".join(pins)}
else:

def stored_sweep(dataset, methods=None):
    """The package's own sweep of `dataset` (`load_results(source="rerun")`) as the object
    `run_all` returns, so `.summary` / `.plot()` work on a host that cannot run the methods."""
    long = mtb.load_results(CATEGORY, dataset=dataset, source="rerun", methods=methods)
    recs = [{"method": m, "status": "STORED", "metrics": g.set_index("metric")["value"].to_dict()}
            for m, g in long.groupby("method")]
    return mtb.BatchResult(recs, dataset, CATEGORY)

def stand_in(dataset, methods, stored):
    """What a host without the method environments shows instead of `run_all`'s result: the benchmark
    host's real `run_all` outputs for `dataset` (`mtb.data.fetch_outputs` - embeddings included), else
    the package's stored metric table (`stored_sweep(*stored)`). One line says which."""
    try:
        res = mtb.load_batch(mtb.data.fetch_outputs(dataset), methods=methods)
        print(f"stand-in: the benchmark host's run_all outputs for {dataset} (fetch_outputs) - real embeddings and run times")

        print(f"stand-in: the package's stored metric table ({type(e).__name__} from fetch_outputs: {e})")
        return stored_sweep(*stored)

  rna1.h5 rna2.h5 atac2.h5 atac3.h5   <- numbered, one per batch

Modality roles and the filenames they resolve to:
    rna              rna.h5      - gene expression
    adt              adt.h5      - surface protein (CITE-seq antibody-derived tags)
    atac             atac.h5     - chromatin accessibility
    atac_gas         atac.h5     - ATAC as GENE-ACTIVITY scores  <-- note: plain atac.h5
    atac_peak        peak.h5     - ATAC as PEAKS                 <-- note: peak.h5, NOT atac.h5
    rna1/rna2/...    rna1.h5, rna2.h5, ... - one file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)
    adt1/adt2/...    adt1.h5, adt2.h5, ... - one file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)
    cty              cty.csv     - cell-type labels, ONE label set (vertical)
    rna_cty / atac_cty rna_cty.csv, atac_cty.csv - one label file PER MODALITY, used when RNA and ATAC come from different cells (diagonal)
    cty1/cty2/...    cty1.csv, cty2.csv, ... - one label file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)

!! ATAC: the role name does NOT guarantee the representation.
   atac_gas resolves to atac_gas.h5 if present, otherwise FALLS BACK
   to atac.h5 - and in the shipped multiome datasets (D12-D17) atac.h5
   contains PEAKS, not gene activity. Only D27/D28 ship a real
   atac_gas.h5. Verified by feature names: 12 atac.h5 files are peaks
   (chr1:3094772-3095489), 2 atac_gas.h5 files are gene activity.
   atac_peak resolves to atac_peak.h5, else peak.h5.
   This matters because methods disagree (lists from the registry;
   see mtb.find_methods(atac=...) / mtb.method_info(m)['atac']):
     need GENE ACTIVITY: SCALEX/scBridge/scMDC/Matilda/VIPCCA/Portal/uniPort/sciCAN/scJoint/UnitedNet/iNMF/online_iNMF/Conos
     need PEAKS:         Multigrate/Seurat_v5/MultiVI/Cobolt/scMVP/scMM/scMoMaT/moETM/MIRA/VIMCCA/SMILE/GLUE/MultiMAP/iPOLNG/StabMap/Seurat_v3/Seurat_WNN
   Feeding the wrong one runs to completion and returns a plausible
   but WRONG embedding - no error.
   Check what you actually have before trusting a cross-dataset result.
   scan() flags the commonest trap in its `caveat` column: an atac_gas
   role that fell back to an atac.h5 whose features are chr:start-end.

MODALITY FILE FORMAT (.h5) - easiest route first:
  mtb.io.to_canonical(src, dst)   converts an .h5ad and writes
  everything below correctly. Prefer it over building the file by hand.
  For a whole dataset in one call (every modality + labels, numbered
  per batch when batch= is given):
    mtb.io.export_dataset(adata, '<data_path>/MYDATA', rna='X',
                          adt='obsm:protein', labels='obs:cell_type')
  Both store matrix/data as float64, gzip-compressed and chunked, like
  the shipped files (a 3000x2000 8%-dense matrix is ~1.5 MB on disk).

  If you do build it yourself, ALL THREE datasets are required:
    matrix/data      the matrix, stored FEATURES x CELLS
    matrix/features  one entry per feature (row of matrix/data)
    matrix/barcodes  one entry per cell    (column of matrix/data)
  e.g. 2,000 genes x 5,000 cells -> matrix/data has shape (2000, 5000),
  matrix/features has 2000 entries and matrix/barcodes has 5000.
  NOTE this is the TRANSPOSE of the scanpy/AnnData convention
  (AnnData.X is cells x genes). scan() rejects a transposed file, and
  a file with only matrix/data fails with a KeyError about 'features'.
Labels are a single-column CSV: one header line (typically 'x'),
then one cell-type label per cell; the evaluator reads the first
column and skips the header.

mosaic: Several batches where only SOME share a modality; a paired batch bridges the others.


ENVIRONMENTS
  Every method runs in its OWN conda env (they need mutually
  incompatible framework versions). scan() checks TWO gates per row -
  files_ok (the inputs are on disk, oriented and labelled) and env_ok
  (that conda env exists) - and marks a method runnable only when both
  pass, so a sweep never starts one that cannot finish.
      multibench env doctor          # what is needed / what is missing
      multibench env install --run   # build them all from lockfiles
      multibench env install --methods X --packed --run   # just one

Then:  mtb.scan('MYDATA')  ->  mtb.run_all('MYDATA', '<category>', out_dir=...)

Each modality file is HDF5 with three datasets:

dataset contents shape matrix/data the matrix, features x cells (n_features, n_cells) matrix/features one name per feature (n_features,) matrix/barcodes one id per cell (n_cells,)

That is the transpose of the AnnData convention (AnnData.X is cells x genes); the mtb.io writers below handle it, and scan() rejects a transposed file at preflight rather than letting a method fail half an hour in. The label CSV is a single column with one header line (typically x) and one label per cell, in the same order as matrix/barcodes of the matching modality file. For ATAC, check which representation a method wants - gene-activity scores or peaks - because the wrong one runs to completion and returns a plausible but wrong embedding. The shipped label files, as evaluate will read them - the dict comes back in the benchmark's cell-stacking order (cty; cty1, cty2, ... numerically; rna_cty before atac_cty), so mtb.evaluate(embedding, labels=mtb.labels_for(DATASET), metrics="all") scores a multi-file dataset directly, with each cell's file of origin as its batch. metrics= is the one selection knob: None (the default) computes every applicable metric - the clustering family, plus the batch family whenever a batch vector exists; "clustering" / "batch" / "all" name a family, and a list of codes (["ARI", "NMI"]) names exactly those (batch metrics need batch= or a multi-file labels). A dict you built in any other order must say so with label_order=[...]:

import os, shutil
import h5py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def subsample_dataset(src_dir, dst_dir, frac=0.6, seed=0, max_cells=2000, max_features=5000):
    """Copy a dataset to a new name, keeping a random slice of it.

    Cells: a random ``frac`` of each file's cells, capped at ``max_cells``.
    Files sharing a cell count get the SAME kept-cell index, so modality files
    and their label CSVs stay aligned - which is exactly the property your own
    export pipeline must preserve. Features: files with more than
    ``max_features`` rows (peak matrices) keep a random subset, so the copy
    stays small and fast to write. The output is the canonical layout:
    matrix/data as features x cells, plus matrix/features and matrix/barcodes.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    os.makedirs(dst_dir, exist_ok=True)
    counts, keep = {}, {}
    for fn in sorted(os.listdir(src_dir)):
        p = os.path.join(src_dir, fn)
        if fn.endswith(".h5"):
            with h5py.File(p) as f:
                if "matrix/data" in f:
                    counts[fn] = f["matrix/data"].shape[1]   # features x cells
        elif fn.endswith(".csv"):
            counts[fn] = len(pd.read_csv(p))
    for n in set(counts.values()):
        k = min(max(50, int(n * frac)), max_cells)
        keep[n] = np.sort(rng.choice(n, size=k, replace=False))
    for fn, n in counts.items():
        sp, dp = os.path.join(src_dir, fn), os.path.join(dst_dir, fn)
        idx = keep[n]
        if fn.endswith(".csv"):
            pd.read_csv(sp).iloc[idx].to_csv(dp, index=False)
        else:
            with h5py.File(sp) as f, h5py.File(dp, "w") as g:
                grp = g.create_group("matrix")
                n_feat = f["matrix/data"].shape[0]
                fidx = np.arange(n_feat) if n_feat <= max_features else np.sort(rng.choice(n_feat, size=max_features, replace=False))
                block = f["matrix/data"][fidx, :] if n_feat > max_features else f["matrix/data"][()]   # one fancy index per h5py read
                grp.create_dataset("data", data=np.asarray(block)[:, idx])
                if "matrix/features" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("features", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/features"])[fidx])
                if "matrix/barcodes" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("barcodes", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/barcodes"])[idx])
    return dst_dir
import os, shutil import h5py import numpy as np import pandas as pd def subsample_dataset(src_dir, dst_dir, frac=0.6, seed=0, max_cells=2000, max_features=5000): """Copy a dataset to a new name, keeping a random slice of it. Cells: a random ``frac`` of each file's cells, capped at ``max_cells``. Files sharing a cell count get the SAME kept-cell index, so modality files and their label CSVs stay aligned - which is exactly the property your own export pipeline must preserve. Features: files with more than ``max_features`` rows (peak matrices) keep a random subset, so the copy stays small and fast to write. The output is the canonical layout: matrix/data as features x cells, plus matrix/features and matrix/barcodes. """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) os.makedirs(dst_dir, exist_ok=True) counts, keep = {}, {} for fn in sorted(os.listdir(src_dir)): p = os.path.join(src_dir, fn) if fn.endswith(".h5"): with h5py.File(p) as f: if "matrix/data" in f: counts[fn] = f["matrix/data"].shape[1] # features x cells elif fn.endswith(".csv"): counts[fn] = len(pd.read_csv(p)) for n in set(counts.values()): k = min(max(50, int(n * frac)), max_cells) keep[n] = np.sort(rng.choice(n, size=k, replace=False)) for fn, n in counts.items(): sp, dp = os.path.join(src_dir, fn), os.path.join(dst_dir, fn) idx = keep[n] if fn.endswith(".csv"): pd.read_csv(sp).iloc[idx].to_csv(dp, index=False) else: with h5py.File(sp) as f, h5py.File(dp, "w") as g: grp = g.create_group("matrix") n_feat = f["matrix/data"].shape[0] fidx = np.arange(n_feat) if n_feat <= max_features else np.sort(rng.choice(n_feat, size=max_features, replace=False)) block = f["matrix/data"][fidx, :] if n_feat > max_features else f["matrix/data"][()] # one fancy index per h5py read grp.create_dataset("data", data=np.asarray(block)[:, idx]) if "matrix/features" in f: grp.create_dataset("features", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/features"])[fidx]) if "matrix/barcodes" in f: grp.create_dataset("barcodes", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/barcodes"])[idx]) return dst_dir

scan checks two independent gates per method: files_ok - the folder itself (files present, features x cells orientation, one label per cell) - and env_ok - that method's conda environment exists on this machine. runnable is both; reason says which failed and how to fix it. The file gate runs anywhere, so a laptop without a single environment still tells you whether your layout is right.

Across datasets. A summary needs every method to have results on every dataset it averages over, or absence and performance blur into the same bar. Two mosaic datasets therefore ship swept identically - D45 and D45s (a 60% cell subsample of D45 under a new name) - and require_complete=True keeps only the methods present on both, so the matrix is complete by construction. Each bar is the grand rank: the min-max scaled mean rank across the datasets, with length and colour both carrying it, and Overall is the same statistic over the grand ranks. Both metric families appear because both datasets are multi-batch.
