docs.title: Mosaic integration¶
docs.text:
Mosaic integration has several batches where only some share a modality - an RNA-only batch, an ATAC-only batch, and a paired batch that bridges them. Which methods apply depends on the exact per-batch pattern, so scan() is the source of truth for each dataset.

Reference dataset: D45 (32,151 cells). The stored results shipped with these notebooks were produced on it, so every table here reproduces.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text: pip install multibench-sc is the whole install: the 1.3 MB wheel ships the method registry, the stored result tables, the env lockfiles and the reference metadata. The package alone runs this section, section 3 (scan) and sections 4-5. Running methods (section 2, and run_all in section 3) additionally needs their environments - prebuilt linux-64 archives that need no conda binary - on a Linux host. The flag cell decides: with INSTALL_ENVS = False (the default) Run all is safe anywhere - nothing is downloaded, and a run cell on a host without the environments prints one line and stands in the benchmark host's own results; set it True on Colab or a Linux machine to download the environments in section 2 and run the methods for real. The install cell pins numpy / pandas to what the interpreter already has, so pip never upgrades a host's stack, and defines tick, the recorder behind the timing table at the end of the notebook.

docs.title: Environments - only if you will run methods in this session¶
docs.text: Linux; 2 envs, at least 1.8 GB to download (2 of 2 archives measured); multibench env plan --methods StabMap,scMoMaT prints the per-env sizes. The cell below does nothing unless INSTALL_ENVS = True; then it prints the download the dry run measures and installs the prebuilt archives for the methods this tutorial runs (StabMap, scMoMaT) under mtb.config.DEFAULT.envs_dir (~/.cache/multibench/envs on a host without conda - the archives carry their own interpreters, and run activates a prefix directly, so no conda binary is needed, on Colab included; with conda present the prefix goes to its envs dir and conda run is the fallback: MULTIBENCH_RUN_MODE in the API reference). env.install skips anything already present. Other tiers are one flag away on the command line: multibench env install --category mosaic --packed --run (6 envs, at least 15.6 GB to download (6 of 6 archives measured); multibench env plan --category mosaic prints the per-env sizes), or no flag for the whole benchmark (29 envs; multibench env plan totals them). The archives are linux-64: on macOS / Windows a real install refuses (force=True / --force overrides), which is why the cell checks the platform too. Without the environments, section 3's scan and sections 4-5 work as they are.

docs.title: One call¶
docs.text: One call is the whole pipeline: resolve each method's inputs, run it in its own environment, load the embeddings, score them with scIB metrics. Here StabMap, scMoMaT (on D46, whose layout fits these methods; mosaic layouts vary per dataset). Both run in minutes to tens of minutes on D46 - run_sec in the summary is the measured time on our host. The cell first asks scan whether any of these methods has its environment here; where none does (a laptop, Colab with the flag off) it prints one line and stands in the benchmark host's own run_all outputs for D46 - mtb.data.fetch_outputs downloads the tree run_all wrote there (summary, long table and one embedding per method) and mtb.load_batch(..., methods=) reloads it, so the statuses, run times and the evaluate cell below are real. Offline, or before those outputs are published, a second fallback stands in the package's own sweep of D45 (load_results(source="rerun"), the package's re-execution of every wired method - the paper's own tables are source="published"); either way one printed line says which path was taken and every cell below still renders.

docs.title: 3. Your own data¶
docs.text: The same three calls - scan, run_all, plot - on a folder the package has never seen. A dataset is a folder of flat files named by category:

docs.title: 4. Reading stored results¶
docs.text: Section 2 ran two methods; the package ships the full sweep for D45 - every wired method at default settings, hours of compute - so the paper's figures reproduce from stored results in seconds. load_results reads them back as the tidy frame mtb.plot.bubble takes, and every row says in its source column which sweep it came from. The paper has no scIB tables for mosaic (source="published" raises FileNotFoundError pointing at "rerun"), so the package's sweep (4 methods on D45) is this category's only stored source.

docs.title: What runs on a dataset, and why not¶
docs.text: scan inspects a folder and reports every runnable method - and for the rest, the exact reason (missing file, missing environment, wrong layout). Nothing executes. From the shell, multibench scan DATASET --category CATEGORY prints the compact table (method, modalities, runnable, files_ok, env_ok, runtime_tier, reason); --columns all or --format csv|tsv|json gives every column - including command, the exact shell line run() would execute for every variant whose inputs resolve (the line to paste into a scheduler job; multibench run-all ... --dry-run prints the same table). Below, the rows the data admits (files_ok), with the environment gate next to them: env_ok is what this machine has, env_reason the install line for what it lacks, and runnable (both gates) stays empty until the environments exist.

docs.title: What each method exposes for tuning¶
docs.text: method_info(m)["supports"] lists a method's variants with how many hyperparameters each exposes on its command line; mtb.params_for(m, CATEGORY, modalities) names them, params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets them in run_all (--param METHOD:KEY=VALUE on the command line; multibench params METHOD prints the same table for every variant). An empty tunable is honest: many upstream scripts hardcode their hyperparameters, and this package never edits upstream code.

docs.title: What the registry knows about a method, and how to cite it¶
docs.text: method_info carries the upstream reference, repository and version next to the run metadata - availability says whether a public install can run it ('public', or 'benchmark-host-only' for SPIRAL, the one method whose script is not published), needs_labels is the any-variant flag (supports[i] has it per variant), and verbose=True adds the long audit notes plus verification, the recorded end-to-end run(s) behind status='verified' ({dataset, category, status, wall_s, ARI, baseline, verdict, note}); mtb.cite emits the benchmark entry plus one per method you ran.

docs.title: The metrics¶
docs.text:
Two families, matching the paper's grouping. All are higher = better, on [0, 1] except ARI (slightly negative at chance level).

family metrics what they measure clustering / bio-conservation ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI does the embedding separate the annotated cell types? batch correction ASW_batch, GC, iLISI (+ opt-in kBET) are the batches mixed within each cell type?

Batch metrics appear only when the dataset has real batches - their absence on a single-batch dataset is correct, not missing data. kBET is computed only when named (mtb.evaluate(..., metrics=["ASW_batch", "GC", "iLISI", "kBET"])) because it is much slower than the rest.

docs.title: Coverage of the paper¶
docs.text: scan() answers "what runs on this dataset"; this answers how many of the methods the paper benchmarks for mosaic the package wires at all. For each one it does not, the registry's own record is printed - the categories it is wired for and the tasks (mtb.list_tasks() vocabulary) its variants are registered under; no variant for this category means the paper scored it here through a task the package does not run.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶
docs.text: symptom meaning fix files_ok False: input files not found a required file is absent the reason names the exact file and lists what IS in the folder env_ok False that method's conda env is not built the reason carries the one-method multibench env install ... command ... looks like cells x features matrix stored transposed re-export with mtb.io.to_canonical / export_dataset a method FAILs in seconds wrong input representation or layout read res.failures.iloc[0]["error"] - the full command line and stderr tail are there a method TIMEOUTs slow, not broken raise timeout=; runtime tiers in scan are measured, not guessed label_order_confidence low several label files fit the cell count check label_order_candidates in the record batch metrics scored against the wrong batches batch_source="file_of_origin" is the label-file rule res.rescore(batch=my_vector) re-scores the stored outputs without re-running

docs.title: Why is UINMF not in mosaic?¶
docs.text: Two verified blockers, recorded in the registry: its upstream script derives the second batch's unshared features from the FIRST batch's object (harmless when both unshared blocks are the same modality, fatal otherwise), and its two-batch shape fits no mosaic dataset shipped here. A method scan() reports as runnable must actually run, so it is deliberately not offered.

docs.title: Next steps¶
docs.text:
• the other three tutorials: vertical, diagonal, cross
  • the hosted interactive explorer: https://shiny.maths.usyd.edu.au/scMultiBench/ - the full benchmark's rankings, browsable without installing anything
  • mtb.recommend(CATEGORY, modalities=[...]) - stored-result ranking with coverage made explicit; methods wired for the category but absent from the chosen source appear with grand_score NaN rather than vanishing
  • mtb.sweep(...) - one method over a range of one hyperparameter

docs.title: Where the time went¶
docs.text: Seconds per stage, as tick recorded them (the install line is ~0 on a kernel that already had the package):

docs.title: Load & plot results
docs.text:
scMultiBench ships the published benchmark metric tables from Liu, Ding et al. (Nature Methods 2025) and the package's own re-run sweeps, alongside the code that drew the figures. This tutorial covers the two functions you need to turn those tables into a publication-ready panel: mtb.load_results reads the stored metric tables into one tidy long frame, and mtb.plot.bubble renders the scIB-style bubble table the paper uses.

TL;DR

import multibench as mtb

df = mtb.load_results("vertical", dataset="D11")                  # the paper's table
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(df, metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"],
                      title="Vertical integration, D11", save="d11.pdf")

The same panel from the shell:

terminal
multibench plot bubble --category vertical --dataset D11 \
    --metrics ARI,NMI,ASW,cLISI --out d11.pdf

docs.title: Step 1, Load a tidy results frame
docs.text:
mtb.load_results walks the stored result tree and returns a single long-format pandas.DataFrame with seven columns - metric, value, method, dataset, category, clustering, source. One row per (method, dataset, metric) cell. This is the shape every downstream function (plot.bubble, plot.bar, recommend, your own groupby/pivot) expects.

import multibench as mtb

df = mtb.load_results(
    "vertical",               # vertical | diagonal | mosaic | cross; None -> every category (the only positional argument)
    dataset="D11",            # None -> every dataset; a list -> several
    methods=None,             # None -> every method present; a name or list (alias tolerant)
    metrics=None,             # None -> every metric; "clustering" / "batch" / "all" -> a family; or ["ARI", "NMI"]
    clustering="default",     # default | louvain | kmeans
    source="published",       # published | rerun | both
)
df.head()
#   metric     value      method dataset  category clustering     source
# 0    NMI  0.792936  Multigrate     D11  vertical    default  published
# 1    ARI  0.759446  Multigrate     D11  vertical    default  published
# 2    ASW  0.656011  Multigrate     D11  vertical    default  published
# ...

docs.title: Category tokens
docs.text:
scMultiBench groups its 40 integration methods into four integration categories. Pass the clean token; the loader maps it to the (space-named) folder on disk for you. A typo raises ValueError listing the valid ones.

Token Integration setting Modalities vertical Paired, the same cells profiled in every modality RNA+ADT, RNA+ATAC, RNA+ADT+ATAC diagonal Unpaired, separate batches bridged by shared features RNA batch + ATAC batch mosaic Overlapping modalities joined through a bridge mixed cross Several fully-matched datasets integrated together matched

docs.title: Published vs re-run tables
docs.text:
Two sources ship in the package, and the source column of every frame says which one a row came from:

source= What it is Datasets "published" (default) the paper's scIB tables (multibench/result/scib_metric/) vertical 23, diagonal 18, cross 7 (D52-D54, D56-D59; tables kept one level down in a run-configuration folder such as MOFA2/filtered3/ are read too); none for mosaic (FileNotFoundError pointing at source="rerun") "rerun" the package's own sweeps - every wired method at default settings, the tables behind the category tutorials (multibench/result/rerun/long_all_<dataset>.csv; source says rerun, the sweep's package version travels in frame.attrs["rerun_version"]) vertical D11/D11s, diagonal D28/D28s, mosaic D45/D45s, cross D52/D52s "both" the concatenation tell them apart by source

The two can differ for the same method and dataset: methods are stochastic, the published sweep ran on other hardware, and the published tables are partial (vertical ships 8 of the paper's methods; cross mostly one method per dataset) while the re-runs cover every wired method for their dataset. Cite the published numbers; use the re-runs to check reproducibility and to compare against your own run, and compare ranks rather than decimals (see Are my numbers comparable?). mtb.results_coverage(category) lists which (dataset, method, clustering, source) combinations exist; mtb.available_datasets(category, source=...) lists the dataset ids that have a stored table (48 across the categories) - result tables, not downloads: the five datasets mtb.data.fetch can download are D11, D28, D45, D46 and D52. A re-run row that most likely failed silently - ARI below 0.01 where the published table scored above 0.2 for the same (category, dataset, method); today Conos on D28 - is flagged by mtb.DegenerateRerunWarning (a UserWarning) whenever source="rerun" or "both" loads it, with the df[df.method != ...] line to drop it before ranking.

cov = mtb.results_coverage("cross")
cov[cov.dataset == "D52"].groupby("source").method.nunique()   # published 1, rerun 8

docs.title: Clustering variants
docs.text:
scIB clustering metrics depend on the upstream clustering. The published tree stores up to three variants per (dataset, method); pick one with clustering=:

Value Reads Meaning "default" metric.csv the paper's default clustering (Leiden), with corrected ASW/iASW/iF1 coalesced in "louvain" metric_louvain.csv Louvain re-clustering "kmeans" metric_kmeans.csv k-means re-clustering

Which variants ship, per category

diagonal ships all three variants for all 18 datasets. vertical ships louvain for a single (dataset, method) pair (D3 / Concerto) and no kmeans; cross ships louvain and kmeans for D56 only (MOFA2, from its nested filtered3/metric_louvain.csv and kmeans/metric_kmeans.csv). Asking for a variant that is not there raises FileNotFoundError naming the file it looked for; point result_path= at a tree that contains it, or keep clustering="default". The re-run sweeps are default only. A result directory named <method>_louvain is reported under the method's canonical id with clustering="louvain" - no method id ever ends in _louvain.

Metric names and method ids are canonicalised

Both a metrics= list and the returned metric column are passed through catalog.canonical_metric, so you can filter with the clean scIB names - ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI (clustering) and ASW_batch, GC, iLISI, kBET (batch) - regardless of how the underlying CSV spelled them; mtb.evaluate emits the same spelling, so a to_long frame concatenates with a stored table without duplicate metric columns. Likewise methods= accepts any alias of a method id ("mofa+" -> MOFA2, "Seurat(WNN)" -> Seurat_WNN). A filter that matches nothing returns an empty frame with a UserWarning listing what is present, so concatenating several calls never breaks on one typo.

These are stored tables, not a live run

To score your own run instead, compute metrics with mtb.evaluate and reshape the wide frame with mtb.to_long(value_df, method=..., dataset=..., category=...) - it emits the same seven columns (clustering="default", source="user"), so it drops straight into plot.bubble next to a stored table. result_path= also accepts a single long CSV (one you saved with to_csv, or a run_all output's long.csv): blank clustering / source cells are filled per row (default / user), source="published" or "both" keeps every row, and any other source value filters on the file's own column - a value the file does not carry raises ValueError listing the ones present.

docs.title: Step 2, Render the scIB bubble table
docs.text:
mtb.plot.bubble takes the long frame and draws the scIB-style bubble table - the grid of circles the paper uses to rank methods. It returns a matplotlib.Figure.

fig = mtb.plot.bubble(
    df,
    metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"],   # column order, left to right (within each family)
    methods=None,                              # None -> every method in df; unknown names raise
    order=None,                                # None -> best first; a list pins those rows on top
    aggregate="dataset",                       # "dataset" | "summary"
    cmap=None,                                 # override the first family's colour ramp
    title="Vertical integration, D11",
    save="d11_bubble.pdf",                     # also returns the Figure
    show_language=True,                        # Py / R chip per row, 'L' badge for label-consuming methods
    require_complete=False,                    # summary: keep only methods present in every dataset
    overall="rank",                            # how the across-dataset Overall is formed (see below)
    na="warn",                                 # a method missing a metric: "warn" (once per build) | "skip" | "raise"
)

How to read it:

  • Each row is a method, each column a metric. Metrics are grouped into the paper's task families - blues for DR & clustering, greens for batch correction - and each family is led by an Overall bar. Rows are ordered by the mean of the family Overall scores, best at the top.
  • Circle fill ~ value - darker = higher, on a per-column min-max scale.
  • Circle radius ~ rank - bigger = better in that column (0.85 * sqrt(rank / n) with n = the methods scored in that column; ties take the maximum rank, matching the original R ties.method="max").
  • The family Overall bar - within one dataset, minmax(mean over the family's metrics of per-metric max-rank); length and fill both carry it.
  • Missing metrics - a dash marks a metric that was not computed for that method (n/a). Its row's Overall averages the ranks of the metrics the method has, and that column's ranks count only the methods scored in it. na="warn" (default) reports each such method once per build_table (YukiNet: DR and clustering Overall over 3 of 4 metrics (cLISI n/a)), na="skip" silences it, na="raise" refuses an incomplete frame; the rule is also printed in the n/a legend line.
  • Legend - a Score colour ramp per family always; the Rank circle-size legend only under aggregate="dataset" (summary panels draw bars); a key line under the legends explains the chips: Py / R = language · L = consumes cell-type labels (supervised) · ? = not a registry method.
  • A ? chip marks a method that is not in the registry (your own), an L badge a method that consumes cell-type labels - supervised, so its scores are not comparable with the unsupervised rows. The badge follows the variants of the frame's category (scMoMaT has no L in a vertical panel); for a method outside the registry, a needs_labels column in the frame (mine["needs_labels"] = True) is what build_table honours.

docs.title: Individual vs. summary panels
docs.text:
The aggregate argument decides what a row's numbers mean.

aggregate=\"dataset\" (individual)aggregate=\"summary\" (across datasets) 
# one dataset -> raw metric values are plotted directly
df = mtb.load_results("vertical", dataset="D11")
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(df, metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"])

The default. Fill encodes the actual metric value for that dataset. If the frame happens to hold several datasets, values are averaged per (method, metric) first, a UserWarning says so, and the row labels carry the dataset ids.

# two vertical datasets swept identically -> rank within each, then average ranks
df = mtb.load_results("vertical", dataset=["D11", "D11s"], source="rerun")
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(df, metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"],
                      aggregate="summary", require_complete=True,
                      title="Vertical integration, summary of D11 + D11s")

Ranks methods within each dataset per metric, then averages those ranks across datasets and draws them as bars - the cross-dataset leaderboard, not a raw mean of incommensurable scores. A method absent from a dataset scores rank 0 there (the paper's rule), which pulls it down; a UserWarning lists such methods, and require_complete=True restricts the panel to methods present in every dataset instead. The re-run pair above is complete by construction (13 methods on both); the published vertical tables are partial, so require_complete=True over all 23 of them leaves a single method - read the coverage warning before trusting any across-dataset order.

The across-dataset Overall: overall=

Two formulas exist and they can order methods differently on the same frame. "rank" (bubble's default, the paper's summary rule): minmax(mean over metrics of max-rank(mean over datasets of within-dataset max-rank)) - absence counts as rank 0. "mean_overall" (bar's default): mean over datasets of minmax(mean over metrics of within-dataset max-rank) - each dataset gets its own min-max-scaled overall, averaged over the datasets the method was actually run on (absence skipped). Pass the same overall= to plot.bubble and plot.bar to get the same ordering; the formula in use is printed on the figure.

Pinning the row order

Pass order=[...] (a list of method ids) to put those rows first, in that order - handy when you want a fixed method order shared across several figures; unlisted methods follow, best first. order= only reorders (an unknown name raises ValueError); methods=[...] subsets the frame before anything is ranked, and metrics= sets the column order within each family. Duplicate (method[, dataset], metric) rows raise rather than being silently averaged - name variants distinctly.

docs.title: Audit the numbers before drawing
docs.text: mtb.plot.build_table(df, ...) (same keywords as bubble minus the drawing ones) returns the BubbleTable behind the figure: methods in row order, overall, matrix (the min-max fills; norm is the same frame), raw, ranks (the per-column max-ranks concatenated over the family blocks in figure order, index == methods, n = best), blocks, aggregate, overall_basis, datasets, coverage, method_datasets, category, needs_labels and na_cells (the missing-metric report). So ranks can be read programmatically - e.g. the position of your own method: mtb.plot.build_table(allruns).methods.index("MyMethod") + 1. Every selector is keyword-only (build_table(df, ["ARI"]) raises TypeError). mtb.plot.render(table, cmap=, title=, show_language=) draws it (importable, not in mtb.plot.__all__).

docs.title: Summary bars
docs.text: mtb.plot.bar(df, group="clustering" | "batch", overall=..., top=N, save=...) draws one bar per method with its across-dataset Overall - the benchmark's two summary panels - with one dot per dataset behind each bar (under overall="mean_overall") so a uniformly good method is distinguishable from one that wins a single dataset.

docs.title: A concrete example, a vertical panel
docs.text:
Reproduce one vertical-integration panel end to end, then add your own method:

reproduce_d11.py
import pandas as pd
import multibench as mtb

# 1. stored table for one dataset - the re-run sweep covers every wired method
bench = mtb.load_results("vertical", dataset="D11", source="rerun")

# 2. your own run, scored with the same metrics (see Evaluate a run)
mine = mtb.to_long(mtb.evaluate(emb, labels=mtb.labels_for("D11")["cty"]),
                   method="MyMethod", dataset="D11", category="vertical")

# 3. bubble table, four clustering metrics, saved to PDF
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(
    pd.concat([bench, mine]),
    metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"],
    title="Vertical integration, D11 + MyMethod",
    save="d11_vertical.pdf",
)
print(mtb.plot.build_table(pd.concat([bench, mine])).methods.index("MyMethod") + 1)   # its rank

The returned fig is a plain matplotlib.Figure, so you can keep tweaking it (fig.axes[0]...), embed it in a multi-panel layout, or re-save at another DPI.

docs.title: CLI equivalent
docs.text:
The same figure without writing any Python:

terminal
multibench plot bubble \
    --category vertical --dataset D11 --source rerun \
    --metrics ARI,NMI,ASW,cLISI \
    --out d11_vertical.pdf

multibench plot accepts --aggregate dataset|summary, --overall rank|mean_overall, --require-complete, --methods, --title, --input long.csv (your own long table, or a run_all output directory; repeatable), bar with --group clustering|batch, and writes whatever format --out's extension implies (.pdf, .png, ...). --input alone plots your table; --input together with --category (and --dataset / --source) concatenates your rows onto the stored table - the CLI form of the pd.concat([bench, mine]) above, with a # overlay: ... note on stderr saying how many rows came from where. It calls load_results and plot.bubble / plot.bar under the hood, so the result is identical to the script above.

Visual fidelity

The bubble table is a matplotlib reproduction of scIB's original R tables (helpers.R / scIB_knit_table.R). The numeric encoding - min-max fills, max-rank radii, the overall bars - is ported verbatim, so rankings and shadings match; the rendering is visually faithful within tolerance rather than a pixel-exact clone of the R figure.

Next: see the API reference for the full load_results, plot.bubble, evaluate, and to_long signatures.

docs.title: Run a method
docs.text:
scMultiBench runs the original, unmodified method scripts from the reference repository - it never edits them. mtb.run reads a method's declaration from the registry, picks the right variant from the inputs you pass, builds the exact command line, runs it inside that method's own conda environment, and loads the typed output back into Python. (mtb.run_all does this for every method that fits a dataset folder, and scores the outputs - the category tutorials are built on it; this page is the single-method call underneath.)

TL;DR

import multibench as mtb

mtb.data.fetch("D28")                          # 137 MB reference dataset; no-op when present
res = mtb.run(
    "SCALEX", "diagonal",
    inputs=mtb.inputs_for("D28", "diagonal", "SCALEX"),   # (dataset, category, method) -> {'rna': .../D28/rna.h5, 'atac_gas': .../D28/atac_gas.h5}
    out_dir="runs/scalex_d28",
)
res.output.shape   # -> (11014, 10)  joint embedding: 6,408 RNA + 4,606 ATAC cells x latent dims

docs.title: The run model
docs.text:
Each method is declared once in the registry (multibench/engine/methods.yaml) as a MethodSpec. A spec lists the categories and tasks the method supports, the conda env it needs, and one variant per (category, modality-set) it can handle. A single mtb.run call walks this path:

  1. Look up the spec for method and collect the modality roles from your inputs (auxiliary roles like data_dir are ignored here).
  2. Select the variant whose when: matches (category, modalities). The match is exact on the set of modality roles - {"rna", "atac_gas"} selects the diagonal RNA + gene-activity variant, not the vertical one.
  3. Preflight the environment: with the default cmd_template, a missing environment - no prefix under envs_dir, no conda env by that name - raises OSError naming the install command before anything is written.
  4. Convert inputs to the canonical scMultiBench .h5 (unless convert=False) into a per-run inputs/ folder.
  5. Build the command - [interpreter, entrypoint, *args, *params] - with the entrypoint resolved against the reference repo_path.
  6. Wrap and execute in the per-run out_dir working directory: the prefix activation when the env is unpacked on disk, conda run -n <env> {cmd} otherwise (how the environment is entered), or your own cmd_template.
  7. Load the output by its declared kind (e.g. an embedding ndarray) into a RunResult.

Each method needs its own conda environment

The env each method needs is declared in the registry - for SCALEX it is scmb_torch (see mtb.method_info("SCALEX")["env"], the same name scan's env column, env doctor and multibench env recipe / yml use) - and it must exist on your machine. Unpack the prebuilt archive (no conda binary needed) or build it from the committed lockfile with multibench env install --methods SCALEX --packed --run (mtb.env.install(["SCALEX"], dry_run=False) from Python); multibench env doctor lists what exists and what is missing. mtb.run enters the env by activating its prefix, or with conda run -n <env> ... when the env is a named conda env only (below); if the env is missing the preflight raises OSError with that install command. multibench run ... --dry-run prints the exact command line without executing it (--param KEY=VALUE merges hyperparameters into it), the line an HPC job can carry; mtb.run(method, category, inputs=..., out_dir=..., dry_run=True) returns the same argv from Python (paths absolutized exactly as a real call passes them, nothing created), and mtb.scan(dataset, category) carries the per-variant form for a laid-out dataset folder in its command column (out_dir defaults to a <out_dir> placeholder for previews).

docs.title: Inputs: roles and format flexibility
docs.text:
inputs is a dict mapping each modality role to a file path (or an in-memory AnnData). Roles are the method's own argument names from the registry - for SCALEX's diagonal variant they are rna and atac_gas (gene-activity scores derived from ATAC). For a benchmark dataset, mtb.inputs_for(dataset, category, method) resolves them for you - the same (dataset, category, ...) order as scan and run_all; the 0.2 (dataset, method, category) order raises TypeError - and check=True verifies the files exist, are oriented features x cells and have one label per cell (the default check=False returns the paths without looking; check=None warns about missing ones). Every path it returns is absolute. When the method has several variants for the category and you pass no modalities, it picks the one whose input files are all in the folder; when none or several are, it raises mtb.AmbiguousVariantError - a ValueError (which also matches KeyError, for older handlers) - listing the modality-sets, the folder's contents and an example modalities=. modalities=["rna", "atac"] selects a variant declared atac_gas or atac_peak too (gas / peak are accepted as aliases).

You do not have to pre-convert your data. By default mtb.run routes every modality input through mtb.io.to_canonical, which adapts common formats to the canonical scMultiBench .h5 (HDF5 with matrix/data as features x cells, matrix/features, matrix/barcodes; sparse matrices are streamed, the file is gzip-compressed). matrix/data is stored dense: cells x features x 8 B uncompressed on disk (dtype="float32" halves it), so filter to highly variable genes / informative peaks before export - a 100k-cell x 200k-peak multiome would be 160 GB; to_canonical warns above 1 GB (mtb.io.DENSE_WARN_BYTES) naming the size and the two mitigations:

Input you pass Handled by to_canonical .h5ad / .h5mu anndata / mudata readers (mod= picks the MuData modality) .csv / .tsv parsed to a matrix (cells x features) .loom anndata.read_loom in-memory AnnData used directly (layer= / obsm= select the matrix) already-canonical .h5 passed through unchanged 
# both inputs become canonical .h5 before the method sees them; the D28
# files are already canonical, so to_canonical passes them through unchanged
mtb.run(
    "SCALEX", "diagonal",
    inputs={"rna": "data/D28/rna.h5", "atac_gas": "data/D28/atac_gas.h5"},
    out_dir="runs/scalex_d28",
)

Pass convert=False when your inputs are already in the exact layout the method expects and you want scMultiBench to hand the paths through verbatim:

mtb.run(..., convert=False)   # no format adaptation; paths used as-is

docs.title: Your own data as a dataset folder
docs.text:
For run_all / scan (and for inputs_for) the inputs live in a dataset folder laid out by category - mtb.describe_layout(category) prints the contract. One call writes it from an AnnData or MuData:

import anndata as ad
a = ad.read_h5ad("my_citeseq.h5ad")                 # X = RNA, obsm['protein'] = ADT, obs['celltype']
mtb.io.export_dataset(a, "data/MYCITE", rna="X", adt="obsm:protein", labels="obs:celltype")
#   -> data/MYCITE/rna.h5, adt.h5, cty.csv; batch="obs:sample" writes rna1.h5/cty1.csv ... per batch
mtb.io.export_dataset(mdata, "data/MYMULTIOME", rna="rna", atac="atac", atac_kind="peak",
                      labels="rna:celltype", category="vertical")   # MuData: bare modality names -> rna.h5, atac.h5, cty.csv
mtb.scan("MYCITE", "vertical", data_path="data")    # files_ok / env_ok per method, with reasons

Or file by file - to_canonical(src, "data/MYDIAG", modality="rna") picks the canonical filename for the modality, the single-column cty CSV is one header line x and one label per cell (pd.Series(labels, name="x").to_csv(path, index=False)), and read_canonical is the inverse (canonical .h5 -> AnnData, cells x genes). The modality argument is validated, and for ATAC it is the one place you say whether the matrix is peaks or gene activity - the two are not interchangeable, see the ATAC note printed by describe_layout. Pass category= with an ATAC matrix: category="vertical" writes plain atac.h5 whatever the representation, because the vertical (paired multiome) methods read the atac role and never open atac_peak.h5 / atac_gas.h5 (the representation is recorded nowhere on disk - feed the one method_info(m)["atac"] wants); diagonal / mosaic / cross keep atac_peak.h5 / atac_gas.h5. inputs_for / scan name a near-miss when they find the other file (atac.h5 not found; found atac_gas.h5 - vertical methods read atac.h5 ...), and scan's caveat column flags an ATAC role resolved to the wrong representation in either direction.

docs.title: Inspecting variants before you run
docs.text:
Use mtb.method_info to see which categories, tasks, environment, and variant entrypoints a method declares - supports lists, per variant, the modality roles it expects and whether it needs labels.

info = mtb.method_info("SCALEX")
info["env"], info["atac"], info["needs_labels"]   # ('scmb_torch', 'gene_activity', False)
info["supports"]
# [{'category': 'diagonal', 'modalities': ['rna', 'atac_gas'],
#   'output_kind': 'embedding', 'n_tunable': 0, 'needs_labels': False}]

If the (category, modalities) you pass has no matching variant, mtb.run raises a KeyError that lists every (category, modality-set) the method does support, so the fix is usually to adjust your inputs keys.

status tells you what is wired

Every registry method has status: "verified": its command template was cross-checked against the real entrypoint and executed end to end on a reference dataset. mtb.method_info(m, verbose=True)["verification"] returns those runs (from the shipped multibench/files/final_verification.tsv) with their ARI, the baseline ARI from first verification and a verdict (DRIFT when a stochastic re-run leaves the tolerance). status says nothing about where the script lives: method_info(m)["availability"] is public for every method but SPIRAL, whose script is not published (benchmark-host-only; scan reports it not runnable); GPSA runs through the package driver engine/drivers/run_gpsa.py and is public.

docs.title: Validated example: SCALEX diagonal integration on D28
docs.text:
This is a real, GPU-validated run (2,233 s on our host - mtb.method_info("SCALEX")["runtime"]). SCALEX performs diagonal integration (unpaired modalities bridged by shared features): an RNA population (rna) and an ATAC population summarised as gene-activity scores (atac_gas) from dataset D28, which mtb.data.fetch("D28") downloads (137 MB).

run_scalex_d28.py
import multibench as mtb

mtb.data.fetch("D28")
res = mtb.run(
    "SCALEX",
    category="diagonal",
    inputs=mtb.inputs_for("D28", "diagonal", "SCALEX", check=True),
    out_dir="/abs/path/runs/scalex_d28",
)

print(res.output.shape)   # -> (11014, 10)   joint embedding (RNA + ATAC cells x latent dims)
print(res.cmd)            # the exact argv that ran, including the conda wrapper

Paths are made absolute for you

The method script runs with out_dir as its working directory (step 6 above), and out_dir is also passed to the script as its save path, so a relative path resolved by the subprocess would land in the wrong place. run therefore makes every path-valued input and out_dir absolute (symlinks preserved) before it builds the command - a directory role such as data_dir also gets its trailing separator - and inputs_for returns absolute paths; RunResult.out_dir is the absolute path. No cmd_template is needed: the wrapper fills the env from the spec (scmb_torch for SCALEX) - the prefix activation or conda run -n scmb_torch - so the run lands in the right environment automatically.

mtb.run returns a RunResult dataclass:

Field Type What it holds method str the method id you ran out_dir Path the per-run working directory cmd list[str] the exact wrapped command line that executed output object the primary loaded output, here an embedding ndarray extra dict any additional declared outputs, keyed by filename stdout / stderr str captured subprocess streams 
res.output            # numpy ndarray, shape (11014, 10), the joint embedding
res.extra             # {} for SCALEX (no extra outputs)
res.cmd[:3]           # ['bash', '-c', '<activate>; exec "$@"'] in prefix mode; [<conda>, 'run', '-n'] in conda mode

The embedding flows straight into evaluation and plotting. D28's labels are two files - one per modality, because the RNA and ATAC cells differ - and passing both as a list makes each cell's file of origin the batch for the batch metrics (see Evaluate a run):

metrics = mtb.evaluate(res.output, labels=mtb.labels_for("D28"),   # {'rna_cty': ..., 'atac_cty': ...} - RNA cells first, then ATAC
                       category="diagonal", metrics="all")         # both families; the default metrics=None does the same here

labels_for returns the files in the benchmark's cell-stacking order (RNA before ATAC; cty1, cty2, ... numerically), which is the order SCALEX stacks the cells, so the dict goes in directly; labels_for("D28", "diagonal", "SCALEX") follows that variant's own modality order. A dict you assembled in another order must pass label_order=[...] (or a list of paths in cell order). run_all finds that order for you and records it as summary.label_order.

docs.title: How the environment is entered: prefix and conda modes
docs.text:
Without a cmd_template, run picks the wrapper per call from what is on disk - and nothing needs a conda binary once the env's prefix exists:

  • prefix mode (the default whenever mtb.env.env_prefix(env) finds one): the argv is bash -c '<activate>; exec "$@"' -- <cmd>, where <activate> sets CONDA_PREFIX=<prefix>, CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV=<env> and PATH=<prefix>/bin:$PATH, and sources every <prefix>/etc/conda/activate.d/*.sh (the R environments ship six; they assume CONDA_PREFIX). python / Rscript in <cmd> then resolve inside the env. The prefix is <envs_dir>/<env> when that folder has a bin/ - envs_dir being mtb.config.DEFAULT.envs_dir: the MULTIBENCH_ENVS_DIR environment variable, else the first writable envs dir of the conda / mamba on PATH, else ~/.cache/multibench/envs - which is where multibench env install --packed --run unpacks the prebuilt archives (relocatable conda-pack archives with their own interpreters; install runs their bin/conda-unpack itself), and otherwise the prefix conda reports for that name when conda is found.
  • conda mode (the fallback when no prefix is on disk but a conda / mamba binary is found): conda run -n <env> <cmd>.

MULTIBENCH_RUN_MODE=conda|prefix forces one mode for every call (prefix forced with no prefix on disk raises OSError naming envs_dir and mtb.env.install); mtb.scan(...)["command"] and multibench run --dry-run show the line the chosen mode would run, so a scheduler job can carry it verbatim. env doctor and scan's env_ok count an env as installed exactly when env_prefix finds it - with or without conda.

docs.title: GPU or CPU?
docs.text:
Most method scripts pick a device themselves (torch.cuda.is_available() fallback, or a library that does the same), so on a CPU-only runtime - a Colab CPU session, a laptop - they simply run slower. Two exceptions are read from each script's source and recorded per method in the registry:

  • method_info(m)["cpu_params"] - the command-line values that turn CUDA off in a script that has it on by default: {'use_cuda': ''} for scJoint (its argparse --use_cuda is type=bool, and bool("False") is true, so only the empty string switches it off) and {'device': 'cpu'} for scMDC. When mtb.env.host_has_gpu() is False, run merges them into params before building the command - run(..., dry_run=True) and scan(...)["command"] show the merged flags - and prints one line to stderr, [run] no GPU on this host: applying scJoint cpu_params {'use_cuda': ''}. A key you pass in params yourself always wins.
  • method_info(m)["requires_gpu"] - the script calls CUDA unconditionally, with no switch (scBridge, moETM, SMILE, sciCAN, UnitedNet, iPOLNG, SPIRAL); method_info(m)["gpu_evidence"] is the file:line of that call. On a host without an NVIDIA GPU run refuses such a method with OSError before launching anything - scBridge needs an NVIDIA GPU: the upstream script calls CUDA unconditionally (tools_scripts/scBridge/main_scBridge.py:46); see method_info(m)["requires_gpu"] - and scan / run_all report the same sentence as that row's env_reason (env_ok=False, runnable=False), so a sweep never starts it. On a GPU host nothing changes.

Neither key says anything about the environment: the torch envs of the tutorial methods are published in a CUDA build and a CPU-only build (<env>-cpu), and mtb.env.install(..., flavor="auto") picks the CPU archive on a GPU-less host by itself - see Archive flavours. A method that runs on CPU needs the CPU archive only to save the download; a requires_gpu method needs the CUDA build and a GPU.

>>> [m for m in mtb.list_methods() if mtb.method_info(m)["requires_gpu"]]
['scBridge', 'moETM', 'SMILE', 'sciCAN', 'UnitedNet', 'SPIRAL', 'iPOLNG']
>>> mtb.method_info("scJoint")["cpu_params"]
{'use_cuda': ''}

docs.title: Choosing a cmd_template
docs.text:
cmd_template decides how the built command is executed; {cmd} is the placeholder for the argv. When you pass none, the two modes above target the method's declared env; the conda-mode wrapper spelled out is:

cmd_template = "conda run -n {env} {cmd}"   # what conda mode runs; {env} filled from the spec

Override it to run elsewhere, e.g. an explicit env name, a Singularity container, or an HPC scheduler wrapper (the env preflight is skipped - you own the environment then):

Explicit conda envSingularity / ApptainerRun in the current env 
mtb.run(..., cmd_template="conda run -n scmb_torch {cmd}")

mtb.run(..., cmd_template="singularity exec multibench.sif {cmd}")

mtb.run(..., cmd_template="{cmd}")   # no wrapper, use the active interpreter

repo_path points at the checkout of the reference scMultiBench method scripts; it defaults to config.DEFAULT.repo_path (auto-provisioned on first run). The variant entrypoint (e.g. tools_scripts/SCALEX/main_SCALEX.py) is resolved relative to it.

docs.title: Reading other output kinds
docs.text:
The primary output is loaded by its declared kind. embedding / imputed / markers / graph outputs come back as numpy arrays; labels as a list of strings; coords as a path you handle yourself. Any additional files a variant declares land in res.extra, keyed by filename.

Graph-output methods do not return an embedding

A few methods emit a cell-graph rather than a coordinate embedding - notably scMoMaT, MIRA, and Seurat_WNN. For these, res.output is the graph representation, not a (cells x dims) embedding, and downstream steps that assume an embedding (e.g. ASW-style metrics) will not apply directly. mtb.method_info(method)["supports"] names each variant's output_kind; run_all scores scMoMaT through the UMAP it also writes (CHAIN_OK_GRAPH_METHOD) and reports Seurat_WNN as RUN_OK_NO_EMBEDDING.

docs.title: Spatial registration
docs.text:
PASTE, PASTE2, SPIRAL and GPSA (task registration, category cross) align spatial slices; their output is aligned coordinates, not an embedding. Availability comes from the registry: PASTE, PASTE2 and GPSA are public (GPSA through the package driver method_info("GPSA")["driver"], engine/drivers/run_gpsa.py), so find_methods(task="registration", available=True) lists those three; SPIRAL is availability="benchmark-host-only" - its script is not published, so a public install cannot fetch or run it and scan says benchmark-host-only: script not published. They take a directory of slices instead of modality files - the role is data_dir (run appends its trailing /), scan() shows their modalities as (data_dir), and you pass no modalities to run_all / inputs_for (a modalities= filter keeps them with a UserWarning; modalities=[] selects exactly them):

<data_path>/MYVISIUM/            (or <data_path>/MYVISIUM/processed/)
    slice_0.h5ad  slice_1.h5ad  ...   one AnnData per slice, >= 2

Each .h5ad needs .X (expression, spots x genes) and .obsm['spatial'] (spot coordinates, spots x 2). GPSA additionally reads obs['Ground_Truth'] (a region / layer label per spot) from every slice: it drives GPSA's own PAA / LTARI / SCS scores, written to <out_dir>/GPSA_aligned_slices/<data_dir_name>_metrics.csv - scan reports GPSA files_ok=False for a slice without that column. The upstream scripts glob data_dir + '*.h5ad' without sorting, so mtb.run stages the slices as sorted, zero-padded symlinks under <out_dir>/inputs/ (which also gives SPIRAL the unique leading token per filename it wants) and writes <out_dir>/slices_manifest.json mapping each aligned_slice_<i> to its source file - the manifest is the authority for which input became which output. PASTE writes its slices without any obs column and PASTE2 rewrites .X (normalize, log1p, HVG subset) before writing, so keep your originals. Output: aligned_slice_<i>.h5ad per slice, so run_all records RUN_OK_NO_EMBEDDING - clustering metrics do not apply, and registration metrics are not wired into mtb.evaluate in this version. scan() checks the directory for >= 2 .h5ad slices with obsm['spatial'] (the files_ok gate), and mtb.describe_layout("cross") prints this contract in full (describe_layout("spatial") points there - it is a task, not a category).

res = mtb.run("PASTE", "cross", inputs={"data_dir": "/abs/path/data/MYVISIUM"},
              out_dir="/abs/path/runs/paste")
res.output            # path to the aligned slices

Next: turn a run's output into scIB metrics in Evaluate a run, then render the bubble table.

def stored_sweep(dataset, methods=None):
    """The package's own sweep of `dataset` (`load_results(source="rerun")`) as the object
    `run_all` returns, so `.summary` / `.plot()` work on a host that cannot run the methods."""
    long = mtb.load_results(CATEGORY, dataset=dataset, source="rerun", methods=methods)
    recs = [{"method": m, "status": "STORED", "metrics": g.set_index("metric")["value"].to_dict()}
            for m, g in long.groupby("method")]
    return mtb.BatchResult(recs, dataset, CATEGORY)

def stand_in(dataset, methods, stored):
    """What a host without the method environments shows instead of `run_all`'s result: the benchmark
    host's real `run_all` outputs for `dataset` (`mtb.data.fetch_outputs` - embeddings included), else
    the package's stored metric table (`stored_sweep(*stored)`). One line says which."""
    try:
        res = mtb.load_batch(mtb.data.fetch_outputs(dataset), methods=methods)
        print(f"stand-in: the benchmark host's run_all outputs for {dataset} (fetch_outputs) - real embeddings and run times")
        return res
    except Exception as e:                                   # offline, or the outputs are not published yet
        print(f"stand-in: the package's stored metric table ({type(e).__name__} from fetch_outputs: {e})")
        return stored_sweep(*stored)

check = mtb.scan("D11", CATEGORY, methods=['Matilda', 'sciPENN', 'scMM'])
if check.env_ok.any():
    res = mtb.run_all("D11", CATEGORY,
                      methods=['Matilda', 'sciPENN', 'scMM'], params={"Matilda": {"epochs": 5}},
                      out_dir="/tmp/tutorial_vertical")
else:
    print("no method environment on this host - the run is skipped; a stand-in computed elsewhere covers it")
    res = stand_in("D11", ['Matilda', 'sciPENN', 'scMM'], stored=("D11", ['Matilda', 'sciPENN', 'scMM']))
tick("run-or-fetch")
res.summary

    atac_gas         atac.h5     - ATAC as GENE-ACTIVITY scores  <-- note: plain atac.h5
    atac_peak        peak.h5     - ATAC as PEAKS                 <-- note: peak.h5, NOT atac.h5
    rna1/rna2/...    rna1.h5, rna2.h5, ... - one file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)
    adt1/adt2/...    adt1.h5, adt2.h5, ... - one file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)
    cty              cty.csv     - cell-type labels, ONE label set (vertical)
    rna_cty / atac_cty rna_cty.csv, atac_cty.csv - one label file PER MODALITY, used when RNA and ATAC come from different cells (diagonal)
    cty1/cty2/...    cty1.csv, cty2.csv, ... - one label file per BATCH (mosaic/cross)

!! ATAC: the role name does NOT guarantee the representation.
   atac_gas resolves to atac_gas.h5 if present, otherwise FALLS BACK
   to atac.h5 - and in the shipped multiome datasets (D12-D17) atac.h5
   contains PEAKS, not gene activity. Only D27/D28 ship a real
   atac_gas.h5. Verified by feature names: 12 atac.h5 files are peaks
   (chr1:3094772-3095489), 2 atac_gas.h5 files are gene activity.
   atac_peak resolves to atac_peak.h5, else peak.h5.
   This matters because methods disagree (lists from the registry;
   see mtb.find_methods(atac=...) / mtb.method_info(m)['atac']):
     need GENE ACTIVITY: SCALEX/scBridge/scMDC/Matilda/VIPCCA/Portal/uniPort/sciCAN/scJoint/UnitedNet/iNMF/online_iNMF/Conos

   but WRONG embedding - no error.
   Check what you actually have before trusting a cross-dataset result.

MODALITY FILE FORMAT (.h5) - easiest route first:
  mtb.io.to_canonical(src, dst)   converts an .h5ad and writes
  everything below correctly. Prefer it over building the file by hand.
  For a whole dataset in one call (every modality + labels, numbered
  per batch when batch= is given):
    mtb.io.export_dataset(adata, '<data_path>/MYDATA', rna='X',
                          adt='obsm:protein', labels='obs:cell_type')
  Both store matrix/data as float64, gzip-compressed and chunked, like
  the shipped files (a 3000x2000 8%-dense matrix is ~1.5 MB on disk).

  If you do build it yourself, ALL THREE datasets are required:
    matrix/data      the matrix, stored FEATURES x CELLS
    matrix/features  one entry per feature (row of matrix/data)
    matrix/barcodes  one entry per cell    (column of matrix/data)
  e.g. 2,000 genes x 5,000 cells -> matrix/data has shape (2000, 5000),
  matrix/features has 2000 entries and matrix/barcodes has 5000.
  NOTE this is the TRANSPOSE of the scanpy/AnnData convention
  (AnnData.X is cells x genes). scan() rejects a transposed file, and
  a file with only matrix/data fails with a KeyError about 'features'.
Labels are a single-column CSV: one header line (typically 'x'),
then one cell-type label per cell; the evaluator reads the first
column and skips the header.

vertical: Several modalities measured in the SAME cells (e.g. CITE-seq RNA+ADT, or 10x multiome RNA+ATAC). Cells are already matched.


ENVIRONMENTS
  Every method runs in its OWN conda env (they need mutually
  incompatible framework versions). scan() checks TWO gates per row -
  files_ok (the inputs are on disk, oriented and labelled) and env_ok
  (that conda env exists) - and marks a method runnable only when both
  pass, so a sweep never starts one that cannot finish.
      multibench env doctor          # what is needed / what is missing
      multibench env install --run   # build them all from lockfiles
      multibench env install --methods X --packed --run   # just one

Then:  mtb.scan('MYDATA')  ->  mtb.run_all('MYDATA', '<category>', out_dir=...)

Each modality file is HDF5 with three datasets:

dataset contents shape matrix/data the matrix, features x cells (n_features, n_cells) matrix/features one name per feature (n_features,) matrix/barcodes one id per cell (n_cells,)

That is the transpose of the AnnData convention (AnnData.X is cells x genes); the mtb.io writers below handle it, and scan() rejects a transposed file at preflight rather than letting a method fail half an hour in. The label CSV is a single column with one header line (typically x) and one label per cell, in the same order as matrix/barcodes of the matching modality file. For ATAC, check which representation a method wants - gene-activity scores or peaks - because the wrong one runs to completion and returns a plausible but wrong embedding. The shipped label files, as evaluate will read them - the dict comes back in the benchmark's cell-stacking order (cty; cty1, cty2, ... numerically; rna_cty before atac_cty), so mtb.evaluate(embedding, labels=mtb.labels_for(DATASET), metrics="all") scores a multi-file dataset directly, with each cell's file of origin as its batch. metrics= is the one selection knob: None (the default) computes every applicable metric - the clustering family, plus the batch family whenever a batch vector exists; "clustering" / "batch" / "all" name a family, and a list of codes (["ARI", "NMI"]) names exactly those (batch metrics need batch= or a multi-file labels). A dict you built in any other order must say so with label_order=[...]:

The cap keeps the copy small enough to write in seconds on Colab (the full peak matrix of a mosaic dataset is several GB dense).

import os, shutil
import h5py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def subsample_dataset(src_dir, dst_dir, frac=0.6, seed=0, max_cells=2000, max_features=5000):
    """Copy a dataset to a new name, keeping a random slice of it.

    Cells: a random ``frac`` of each file's cells, capped at ``max_cells``.
    Files sharing a cell count get the SAME kept-cell index, so modality files
    and their label CSVs stay aligned - which is exactly the property your own
    export pipeline must preserve. Features: files with more than
    ``max_features`` rows (peak matrices) keep a random subset, so the copy
    stays small and fast to write. The output is the canonical layout:
    matrix/data as features x cells, plus matrix/features and matrix/barcodes.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    os.makedirs(dst_dir, exist_ok=True)
    counts, keep = {}, {}
    for fn in sorted(os.listdir(src_dir)):
        p = os.path.join(src_dir, fn)
        if fn.endswith(".h5"):
            with h5py.File(p) as f:
                if "matrix/data" in f:
                    counts[fn] = f["matrix/data"].shape[1]   # features x cells
        elif fn.endswith(".csv"):
            counts[fn] = len(pd.read_csv(p))
    for n in set(counts.values()):
        k = min(max(50, int(n * frac)), max_cells)
        keep[n] = np.sort(rng.choice(n, size=k, replace=False))
    for fn, n in counts.items():
        sp, dp = os.path.join(src_dir, fn), os.path.join(dst_dir, fn)
        idx = keep[n]
        if fn.endswith(".csv"):
            pd.read_csv(sp).iloc[idx].to_csv(dp, index=False)
        else:
            with h5py.File(sp) as f, h5py.File(dp, "w") as g:
                grp = g.create_group("matrix")
                n_feat = f["matrix/data"].shape[0]
                fidx = np.arange(n_feat) if n_feat <= max_features else np.sort(rng.choice(n_feat, size=max_features, replace=False))
                block = f["matrix/data"][fidx, :] if n_feat > max_features else f["matrix/data"][()]   # one fancy index per h5py read
                grp.create_dataset("data", data=np.asarray(block)[:, idx])
                if "matrix/features" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("features", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/features"])[fidx])
                if "matrix/barcodes" in f:
                    grp.create_dataset("barcodes", data=np.asarray(f["matrix/barcodes"])[idx])
    return dst_dir

docs.title: Vertical integration¶
docs.text:
Vertical integration fuses several modalities measured in the same cells (here CITE-seq: RNA + surface protein). Cells are already matched, so the task is combining modalities, not aligning cells.

Reference dataset: D11 (2,864 cells). The stored results shipped with these notebooks were produced on it, so every table here reproduces.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text: pip install multibench-sc is the whole install: the 1.3 MB wheel ships the method registry, the stored result tables, the env lockfiles and the reference metadata. The package alone runs this section, section 3 (scan) and sections 4-5. Running methods (section 2, and run_all in section 3) additionally needs their environments - prebuilt linux-64 archives that need no conda binary - on a Linux host. The flag cell decides: with INSTALL_ENVS = False (the default) Run all is safe anywhere - nothing is downloaded, and a run cell on a host without the environments prints one line and stands in the benchmark host's own results; set it True on Colab or a Linux machine to download the environments in section 2 and run the methods for real. The install cell pins numpy / pandas to what the interpreter already has, so pip never upgrades a host's stack, and defines tick, the recorder behind the timing table at the end of the notebook.

docs.title: Environments - only if you will run methods in this session¶
docs.text: Linux; 3 envs, at least 1.5 GB to download (3 of 3 archives measured); multibench env plan --methods Matilda,scMM,sciPENN prints the per-env sizes. The cell below does nothing unless INSTALL_ENVS = True; then it prints the download the dry run measures and installs the prebuilt archives for the methods this tutorial runs (Matilda, scMM, sciPENN) under mtb.config.DEFAULT.envs_dir (~/.cache/multibench/envs on a host without conda - the archives carry their own interpreters, and run activates a prefix directly, so no conda binary is needed, on Colab included; with conda present the prefix goes to its envs dir and conda run is the fallback: MULTIBENCH_RUN_MODE in the API reference). env.install skips anything already present. Other tiers are one flag away on the command line: multibench env install --category vertical --packed --run (18 envs, at least 48.1 GB to download (18 of 18 archives measured); multibench env plan --category vertical prints the per-env sizes), or no flag for the whole benchmark (29 envs; multibench env plan totals them). The archives are linux-64: on macOS / Windows a real install refuses (force=True / --force overrides), which is why the cell checks the platform too. Without the environments, section 3's scan and sections 4-5 work as they are.

docs.title: One call¶
docs.text: One call is the whole pipeline: resolve each method's inputs, run it in its own environment, load the embeddings, score them with scIB metrics. Here Matilda, sciPENN, scMM. Matilda at 5 epochs is quick - run_sec in the summary is the measured time on our host. The cell first asks scan whether any of these methods has its environment here; where none does (a laptop, Colab with the flag off) it prints one line and stands in the benchmark host's own run_all outputs for D11 - mtb.data.fetch_outputs downloads the tree run_all wrote there (summary, long table and one embedding per method) and mtb.load_batch(..., methods=) reloads it, so the statuses, run times and the evaluate cell below are real. Offline, or before those outputs are published, a second fallback stands in the same methods from the package's own sweep of D11 (load_results(source="rerun"), the package's re-execution of every wired method - the paper's own tables are source="published"); either way one printed line says which path was taken and every cell below still renders.

docs.title: 3. Your own data¶
docs.text: The same three calls - scan, run_all, plot - on a folder the package has never seen. A dataset is a folder of flat files named by category:

docs.title: 4. Reading stored results¶
docs.text: Section 2 ran three methods; the package ships the full sweep for D11 - every wired method at default settings, hours of compute - so the paper's figures reproduce from stored results in seconds. load_results reads them back as the tidy frame mtb.plot.bubble takes, and every row says in its source column which sweep it came from. The paper's table for D11 holds 6 methods against 13 in the package's sweep, so the default source="published" would show 6 - every call in this notebook names its source.

docs.title: What runs on a dataset, and why not¶
docs.text: scan inspects a folder and reports every runnable method - and for the rest, the exact reason (missing file, missing environment, wrong layout). Nothing executes. From the shell, multibench scan DATASET --category CATEGORY prints the compact table (method, modalities, runnable, files_ok, env_ok, runtime_tier, reason); --columns all or --format csv|tsv|json gives every column - including command, the exact shell line run() would execute for every variant whose inputs resolve (the line to paste into a scheduler job; multibench run-all ... --dry-run prints the same table). Below, the rows the data admits (files_ok), with the environment gate next to them: env_ok is what this machine has, env_reason the install line for what it lacks, and runnable (both gates) stays empty until the environments exist.

docs.title: What each method exposes for tuning¶
docs.text: method_info(m)["supports"] lists a method's variants with how many hyperparameters each exposes on its command line; mtb.params_for(m, CATEGORY, modalities) names them, params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets them in run_all (--param METHOD:KEY=VALUE on the command line; multibench params METHOD prints the same table for every variant). An empty tunable is honest: many upstream scripts hardcode their hyperparameters, and this package never edits upstream code.

docs.title: What the registry knows about a method, and how to cite it¶
docs.text: method_info carries the upstream reference, repository and version next to the run metadata - availability says whether a public install can run it ('public', or 'benchmark-host-only' for SPIRAL, the one method whose script is not published), needs_labels is the any-variant flag (supports[i] has it per variant), and verbose=True adds the long audit notes plus verification, the recorded end-to-end run(s) behind status='verified' ({dataset, category, status, wall_s, ARI, baseline, verdict, note}); mtb.cite emits the benchmark entry plus one per method you ran.

docs.title: The metrics¶
docs.text:
Two families, matching the paper's grouping. All are higher = better, on [0, 1] except ARI (slightly negative at chance level).

family metrics what they measure clustering / bio-conservation ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1, cLISI does the embedding separate the annotated cell types? batch correction ASW_batch, GC, iLISI (+ opt-in kBET) are the batches mixed within each cell type?

Batch metrics appear only when the dataset has real batches - their absence on a single-batch dataset is correct, not missing data. kBET is computed only when named (mtb.evaluate(..., metrics=["ASW_batch", "GC", "iLISI", "kBET"])) because it is much slower than the rest.

docs.title: Coverage of the paper¶
docs.text: scan() answers "what runs on this dataset"; this answers how many of the methods the paper benchmarks for vertical the package wires at all. For each one it does not, the registry's own record is printed - the categories it is wired for and the tasks (mtb.list_tasks() vocabulary) its variants are registered under; no variant for this category means the paper scored it here through a task the package does not run.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶
docs.text: symptom meaning fix files_ok False: input files not found a required file is absent the reason names the exact file and lists what IS in the folder env_ok False that method's conda env is not built the reason carries the one-method multibench env install ... command ... looks like cells x features matrix stored transposed re-export with mtb.io.to_canonical / export_dataset a method FAILs in seconds wrong input representation or layout read res.failures.iloc[0]["error"] - the full command line and stderr tail are there a method TIMEOUTs slow, not broken raise timeout=; runtime tiers in scan are measured, not guessed label_order_confidence low several label files fit the cell count check label_order_candidates in the record batch metrics scored against the wrong batches batch_source="file_of_origin" is the label-file rule res.rescore(batch=my_vector) re-scores the stored outputs without re-running

docs.text: Seconds per stage, as tick recorded them (the install line is ~0 on a kernel that already had the package):
